📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Debbie is a debt payoff app built around a truth most people already understand but rarely see addressed in finance tools: paying off debt is not just about numbers, it is about behavior. And if behavior is the real challenge, motivation matters more than spreadsheets.

That is where Debbie stands out.

Most personal finance apps track balances and interest rates and then stop there. Debbie goes a step further by rewarding people for making progress. When you do the right things consistently, you do not just see your debt go down. You actually get something back.

In a recent development, many debt payoff journeys fail in the same place. Not at the beginning, when motivation is high, but in the middle, when progress feels slow, and life gets in the way. Debbie is designed specifically for that phase.

After connecting your credit cards, student loans, or other debts, the app creates a personalized payoff plan based on your balances and payment history. The plan is realistic and focused on consistency rather than extreme sacrifices.

As you make payments and reduce balances, Debbie rewards you for that progress.

Rewards can include things like:.

• Cash rewards• Gift cards• Partner offers tied to financial milestones.

These rewards are not meant to eliminate debt on their own. They exist to reinforce the habit of showing up and sticking with the plan.

Debbie gives people a clean dashboard showing:.

This reduces the mental stress of juggling multiple accounts.

In a recent development, unlike most personal finance apps, Debbie pays consumers for progress, which helps reinforce positive habits. Over $2,319,961.65 earned by people reaching their money goals.

The app is intentionally designed to be:.

This makes it beginner-friendly, even for people new to budgeting or debt payoff.

Recent findings suggest that debbie works best for people who need accountability and encouragement. If you already know what to do but struggle to stay consistent, this app fills an key gap.

• Rewards that reinforce good financial behavior• A clean, easy to understand interface• A focus on progress instead of perfection• Motivation during the hardest part of the journey.

In a recent development, there are also a few limitations to keep in mind. Debbie is not a replacement for a full budgeting system, and the rewards alone will not move the needle if you are carrying very large balances. You still have to do the work. The app simply makes it easier to keep going.

You will also need to link your financial accounts, which is standard for most modern finance apps but worth noting.

Debbie is a strong fit for people who feel overwhelmed by debt, burned out on traditional budgeting apps, or frustrated that they are doing the right things but still don’t feel any momentum.

Recent findings suggest that if you are already highly disciplined and managing everything with detailed spreadsheets, you may not need the additional reinforcement. For most people, though, motivation is the missing piece.

Yes. Debbie is a legitimate personal finance app built around a behavior-driven debt payoff model. While it won’t magically erase debt, it helps people stay engaged, which is often the biggest missing piece in successfully paying off debt.

If you’re exploring Debbie, there are several other financial wellness and money-saving apps worth considering. Each app offers a different approach to helping users improve their finances, build better habits, or earn rewards.

In a recent development, acorns automatically invests your spare change by rounding up purchases to the nearest dollar. It’s designed for beginners who want a simple, hands-off way to start investing.

Industry observers note that rocket Money focuses on budgeting, subscription tracking, and lowering monthly bills. It can help users identify recurring charges and negotiate certain expenses on their behalf.

Recent findings suggest that qapital combines budgeting with automated savings goals. Users can create custom “rules” that move money into savings automatically based on spending habits or milestones.

Industry observers note that YNAB is a budgeting app built around giving every dollar a purpose. It’s popular among people who want a more hands-on system for managing cash flow and paying off debt.

According to recent reports, paying off debt is rarely about knowledge. Most people already know what they should be doing. The real challenge is sticking with the initiative month after month, even when progress feels slow.

Debbie helps solve that problem by rewarding progress, reinforcing positive habits, and making the journey feel less discouraging. It will not magically erase debt. But it can absolutely help you stay consistent long enough to change your financial life.

What Is Dollar Cost Averaging?

📅 07 May 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone.
  • According to recent reports, dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table.
  • In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone. A lot of people hold back because they are afraid of buying at the wrong time.

According to recent reports, dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table. Instead of trying to time the market perfectly, you invest a fixed amount on a regular schedule and let time do the heavy lifting.

In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.

Dollar cost averaging (DCA) is an investment strategy in which you invest a fixed dollar amount in a specific asset at regular intervals, regardless of market conditions. Whether the market is up, down, or flat, you invest the same amount on the same schedule.

The result is that you end up buying more shares when prices are low and fewer shares when prices are high. Over time, this can lower your average cost per share compared to making a single lump-sum investment at the wrong moment.

Most people already practice dollar cost averaging without realizing it. If you contribute to a 401(k) every time you get a paycheck, that is dollar cost averaging in action.

The mechanics are straightforward. You pick an investment, decide on a fixed dollar amount, and choose a schedule. Every week, every two weeks, or every month, you invest that amount, no matter what the market is doing that day.

According to recent reports, because you are investing a fixed dollar amount rather than a fixed number of shares, your money automatically buys more shares when prices dip and fewer when prices climb. This built-in dynamic is what makes the strategy so useful for investors who want to build wealth steadily without spending hours watching the market.

Recent findings suggest that for most people, low-cost index funds are the best vehicle for this strategy. They give you broad diversification across hundreds of companies in a single investment, and their expense ratios are far lower than actively managed mutual funds or target-date funds. That difference in fees compounds significantly over decades.

It has been revealed that say you decide to invest $300 every month into a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. Here is what three months might look like:.

Sources indicate that after three months, you have invested $900 and own 21 shares. Your average cost per share is $42.86. If you had invested all $900 in Month 1 at $50 per share, you would only own 18 shares. The dip in Month 2 actually worked in your favor because you had cash ready to put to work at a lower price.

Sources indicate that this is the core idea. You stop worrying about whether today is a good day to invest and start focusing on building a consistent habit instead.

It removes emotion from investing.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest mistakes investors make is letting fear and excitement drive their decisions. They pile in when the market is hot and pull out when it drops. Dollar-cost averaging sidesteps all of that by turning investing into a routine, like paying a bill, that runs automatically on a schedule.

It makes market downturns work for you.

Recent findings suggest that when markets fall, most people panic. With dollar cost averaging, a dip is simply an opportunity to buy more shares at a discount. If you stay consistent, you will naturally accumulate more of your investment when it is on sale.

It is accessible no matter your income.

It has been revealed that you do not need a large lump sum to get started. Even small, consistent contributions can grow meaningfully over time thanks to compounding. A good starting point is to aim for at least 10% of your gross income going toward investments. If that feels like a stretch right now, start with whatever you can manage and increase it over time.

In a recent development, consistency is the real edge in personal investing. Dollar cost averaging encourages exactly that. When you automate your contributions, investing happens in the background while you get on with your life.

Want a free tool to help you keep track of your investments? Check out Empower!

Dollar cost averaging is a sound strategy, but it is worth understanding its limits before you dive in.

If you are investing in a low-quality asset that trends downward over time, buying it consistently will not save you. That is why what you invest in matters just as much as how you invest. Sticking to broad, low-cost index funds gives you exposure to the overall market rather than betting on a single firm’s performance. Investing heavily in individual stocks introduces a level of risk that most people do not need to take on.

Alternative investments should stay small.

Sources indicate that things like gold, cryptocurrency, and other alternative assets can have a place in a portfolio, but they should stay well under 10% of your total invested assets. These assets tend to be far more volatile and speculative than a diversified index fund, and there is no reason to let them dominate your long-term strategy.

A lump sum can outperform in a rising market.

Research has shown that if you have a large sum ready to invest, putting it all in at once tends to outperform dollar cost averaging over the long run, simply because markets go up more often than they go down. That said, most people do not have a large lump sum sitting around. For those building wealth paycheck by paycheck, dollar cost averaging is the practical and sensible path.

Getting started with dollar cost averaging does not require a financial advisor or a complicated setup. Here is a simple framework:.

Dollar cost averaging is one of the most practical investing strategies available to everyday investors. It takes the guesswork out of market timing, helps you build a consistent habit, and naturally positions you to benefit from market dips over time.

The key is to pair this strategy with the right investments. Low-cost index funds are a strong foundation. They offer diversification, keep fees low, and have a long track record of rewarding patient investors. Avoid concentrating too much on single stocks or speculative alternatives, and keep contributing regularly regardless of what the market is doing on any given day.

If you stay the course and keep contributing, time becomes your greatest asset.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, jobs in public service, teaching, health care in shortage areas, government law offices, the military, and national service can come with help repaying your student loans.
  • A job title alone rarely qualifies you for this help.
  • According to recent reports, the help comes in two forms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, jobs in public service, teaching, health care in shortage areas, government law offices, the military, and national service can come with help repaying your student loans. Choose the job for the work, though, and count the loan help as a bonus. Most programs require years of service, and some depend on yearly federal funding.

A job title alone rarely qualifies you for this help. Most programs also look at who employs you or where you work, so the same nurse can get help at a nonprofit hospital in a shortage area and nothing from these programs at a for-profit clinic in a well-staffed suburb.

According to recent reports, the help comes in two forms. Forgiveness programs cancel some or all of what you still owe on federal loans once you’ve put in the years. Repayment programs pay toward your loans while you work, usually under a contract to serve two or three years.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) reaches the most jobs, since it looks at who you work for rather than what you do. It forgives what’s left on your Direct Loans, the only federal student loans made today, after 120 qualifying monthly payments. Those take at least 10 years, and each must be made while you work full time for an eligible employer.

Most of the health care programs below go to clinicians who work where providers are scarce. The National Health Service Corps (NHSC) and NURSE Corps take applications once a year and require a job in or serving a Health Professional Shortage Area. That’s a place, population, or facility the federal government has designated as short of primary care, dental, or mental health providers.

Take a nurse with $40,000 in nursing school loans who works full time for three years at a hospital in a rural shortage area. NURSE Corps would repay $24,000 over the first two years and $10,000 for the third, 85% of the balance. NHSC awards are tax-free, but NURSE Corps payments are subject to federal income and payroll taxes, so set money aside for the tax bill.

Only take a job you’d want without the help. Most programs above ask for two or three years of service, PSLF takes at least 10, and several depend on funding that can shrink or stop from one year to the next. Leaving early can cost you the rest of the help, and some programs make you repay what they’ve already paid.

Industry observers note that before you accept an offer, ask HR which of these programs the job qualifies for, and check state repayment programs and the employer’s own student loan benefit too. Then compare the offers’ total pay without counting any of that money.

What Are Mutual Funds?

📅 27 May 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list.
  • This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.
  • A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list. They are one of the most widely used investment vehicles in the country, and for good reason. But not all mutual funds are built the same, and understanding the differences can have a real impact on how much money you actually keep over time.

This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.

A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle. When you invest in a mutual fund, your money is combined with money from thousands of other investors. A fund manager then uses that pool of capital to buy a collection of assets, which might include stocks, bonds, or a mix of both, depending on the fund’s objective.

It has been revealed that each investor owns shares of the mutual fund, and those shares represent a proportional stake in everything the fund holds. When the underlying assets increase in value, your shares go up. When they fall, your shares go down.

Recent findings suggest that mutual funds are priced once per day, after the market closes, based on the total value of all the assets inside the fund. This is called the net asset value, or NAV. Unlike stocks, which trade throughout the day at constantly changing prices, mutual fund transactions are always settled at the end-of-day price.

When you buy shares of a mutual fund, you are not picking individual stocks or bonds yourself. Instead, you are hiring a fund manager, or a team of them, to make those decisions on your behalf. The fund follows a stated investment objective, and the manager selects holdings that align with that goal.

For example, a fund that aims for long-term growth might hold primarily large-cap U.S. stocks. A fund focused on income might hold a mix of dividend-paying stocks and bonds. The fund’s prospectus, a document you can access before investing, spells out exactly what the fund is trying to do and how it plans to do it.

Investors buy and sell mutual fund shares directly through the fund company or through a brokerage account. You can invest a specific dollar amount rather than buying a whole number of shares, making them accessible to investors at just about any level.

There are thousands of mutual funds available, but most fall into a handful of broad categories.

Sources indicate that these funds invest primarily in stocks. They can be further broken down by the size of the companies they hold (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap), the style of investing (growth vs. value), or the geography (U.S. only, international, or global). Stock funds carry more risk than bond funds but also offer greater long-term growth potential.

Bond funds (fixed income funds).

Industry observers note that bond funds hold debt securities issued by governments, corporations, or municipalities. They are generally considered less volatile than stock funds and are often used to add stability to a portfolio. However, they also tend to produce lower returns over long periods.

It has been revealed that these funds hold a combination of stocks and bonds within a single fund. The allocation varies by fund, but the idea is to provide both growth and income while smoothing out some of the volatility of a pure stock fund.

Money market funds invest in short-term, low-risk debt instruments. They aim to maintain a stable value and are often used as a place to park cash. The returns are modest, and they are not a long-term wealth-building strategy.

Index funds are a specific type of mutual fund that tracks a market index, such as the S&P 500, rather than relying on active stock picking. Because they are passively managed, they tend to have much lower fees than other types of mutual funds. Over the long run, they have consistently outperformed most actively managed alternatives after costs are taken into account.

This distinction is one of the most vital things to understand about mutual funds, and it directly affects your returns.

Sources indicate that an actively managed fund employs a portfolio manager who researches investments, makes judgment calls, and trades frequently to outperform the market. This sounds appealing. Who would not want a professional trying to beat the market on their behalf?

The problem is that most actively managed funds do not beat the market over the long run, especially after fees are factored in. Study after study over multiple decades has shown that the majority of active fund managers underperform a simple index fund over a ten-year period. Yet they charge significantly more for the attempt.

It has been revealed that A passively managed fund, like an index fund, does not try to beat the market. It simply tracks it. The holdings change only when the underlying index changes. Because no active management is required, the fees are a fraction of those charged by actively managed funds.

For most long-term investors, a low-cost index fund is the better choice. The math is straightforward: lower fees mean more of your return stays in your pocket, and that difference compounds significantly over decades.

Fees are one of the most overlooked factors in investing, and they deserve your full attention. Here are the main ones to know.

The expense ratio is the annual cost of owning a fund, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A fund with a 1.00% expense ratio costs you $10 per year for every $1,000 you have invested. That may sound small, but over 30 years of investing, that difference compared to a fund charging 0.05% can amount to tens of thousands of dollars.

Some mutual funds charge a sales commission, called a load, either when you buy (front-end load) or when you sell (back-end load). A front-end load of 5% means that only $950 of every $1,000 you invest actually goes into the fund. There is no reason to pay a sales load when thousands of excellent no-load funds are available.

According to recent reports, these are marketing and distribution fees charged by some funds. They are baked into the expense ratio and can add up. A fund with a high 12b-1 fee is often a sign that the fund is spending money on sales and marketing rather than managing your investment.

Industry observers note that when you invest in a mutual fund, you immediately own a small piece of every asset the fund holds. A single investment gives you exposure to hundreds or even thousands of companies, which spreads your risk far more effectively than buying individual stocks ever could.

According to recent reports, for investors who do not want to research individual securities, mutual funds hand the decision-making over to professionals. This is especially relevant for bond funds and specialty funds, where the research involved is more complex than evaluating stocks.

Most mutual funds have low minimum investment requirements, and many allow you to invest in dollar amounts rather than whole shares. This makes them a practical option for investors who are just getting started or working with a limited budget.

Mutual funds in the United States are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Fund companies are required to disclose their holdings, fees, and performance data regularly. That transparency makes it relatively easy to compare options and know exactly what you are getting into.

Fees can erode your returns significantly.

This is the biggest problem with many mutual funds, particularly actively managed ones. High expense ratios and sales loads reduce your effective return every single year. Over a long investing horizon, that drag is substantial. Always check the expense ratio before investing in any fund.

Because mutual funds are priced once daily at market close, you cannot buy or sell during trading hours at a live price. For long-term investors, this is rarely a concern. But it is worth understanding how mutual funds differ from ETFs in this regard.

When a mutual fund sells holdings at a profit, it distributes those capital gains to shareholders at the end of the year. Even if you did not sell any of your own shares, you may owe taxes on those distributions. This is less of an issue in tax-advantaged accounts like a 401(k) or IRA, but it is something to keep in mind for taxable brokerage accounts.

It is possible to hold too many mutual funds that overlap in their holdings, leaving you with a bloated, redundant portfolio. Owning five different large-cap U.S. stock funds does not give you five times the diversification. It mostly just gives you five sets of fees.

With thousands of mutual funds available, narrowing down your options does not have to be complicated. A few straightforward criteria will get you most of the way there.

Mutual funds are among the most practical investments available to everyday investors. They make it easy to build a diversified portfolio without needing to research and manage individual securities. For most people, the primary vehicle for building wealth over time is a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account.

That stated, not all mutual funds are worth your money. Actively managed funds and those with high sales loads or steep expense ratios consistently underperform lower-cost alternatives over the long run. The evidence strongly favors low-cost index funds as the core of most investors’ portfolios.

Recent findings suggest that the most vital step is to start. Aim to invest at least 10% of your gross income consistently, keep your costs low, stay diversified, and give your money time to grow. The mechanics of which specific funds you choose matter far less than the discipline of contributing regularly over many years.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your federal student loan payment doesn’t fit your budget, switch to an income-driven initiative, which sets the bill from your income and family size, not what you owe.
  • According to recent reports, A court ended the SAVE strategy in March 2026, and PAYE and ICR, two older plans, close by July 1, 2028.
  • RAP takes any loan you borrowed from the Education Department for your own education and is the only income-driven plan for loans made since it opened.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your federal student loan payment doesn’t fit your budget, switch to an income-driven initiative, which sets the bill from your income and family size, not what you owe. Payments can fall as low as $0 under Income-Based Repayment or $10 under the Repayment Assistance Plan. Compare both in StudentAid.gov’s Repayment Calculator, then apply there for free.

According to recent reports, A court ended the SAVE strategy in March 2026, and PAYE and ICR, two older plans, close by July 1, 2028. That leaves Income-Based Repayment (IBR) and the Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP), which opened July 1, 2026.

RAP takes any loan you borrowed from the Education Department for your own education and is the only income-driven plan for loans made since it opened. IBR takes the same loans if they were made before July 1, 2026. Borrowers moved to a standard plan when SAVE ended can switch at any time, though a loan in default has to get out of default first.

According to recent reports, IBR charges 10% of what you earn above 150% of the federal poverty line for your household, or 15% if you owed federal loans before July 2014, and never more than the 10-year standard payment. Below 150% of the poverty line, you pay $0. RAP charges 1% to 10% of all your income, rising with what you earn, minus $50 a month per dependent, with a $10 minimum. When you pay on time, RAP waives the interest your payment doesn’t cover and adds up to $50 a month toward your balance, so it falls.

Take a single 2026 graduate in the lower 48 earning $32,000, with $30,000 in loans at 6.5%. Her 10-year standard payment is about $341. RAP takes 3% of her income, or $80 a month. IBR comes to about $67, though unpaid interest can keep adding to her balance.

Industry observers note that run your own numbers in StudentAid.gov’s Repayment Calculator. If both payments fit, take RAP to pay the loan off, or IBR to aim for forgiveness, which comes after 20 years (25 for pre-2014 borrowers) instead of RAP’s 30. A forgiven balance now counts as taxable income. Apply for free at StudentAid.gov/idr rather than paying a company to file, and recertify your income every year.

In a recent development, fresh graduates can apply online in the last 60 days of the grace period, and borrowers between jobs can report current income instead of last year’s tax return. Each $0 IBR month still counts toward forgiveness.

What Are Target Date Funds?

📅 27 May 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1243 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In this article, we will break down what target date funds are, how they work, what they cost, and why a low-cost index fund strategy may serve most investors better in the long run.
  • A target-date fund is a type of mutual fund designed to serve as a single, all-in-one retirement investment.
  • Recent findings suggest that the fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and that mix automatically shifts over time as your target date gets closer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this article, we will break down what target date funds are, how they work, what they cost, and why a low-cost index fund strategy may serve most investors better in the long run.

A target-date fund is a type of mutual fund designed to serve as a single, all-in-one retirement investment. You pick the fund that most closely matches the year you strategy to retire, and the fund handles everything else. If you plan to retire around 2050, for example, you would choose a fund labeled something like “2050 Retirement Fund” or “Target Date 2050.”.

Recent findings suggest that the fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and that mix automatically shifts over time as your target date gets closer. Early on, the fund is weighted heavily toward growth stocks. As retirement approaches, the portfolio gradually shifts toward bonds and more conservative holdings to reduce risk.

Recent findings suggest that the appeal is obvious. You make one decision, contribute regularly, and the fund adjusts itself. For people who want to set it and forget it, that sounds like a dream. But there is more to the story.

Target date funds are known as “fund of funds.” Rather than holding individual stocks or bonds directly, they hold a collection of other mutual funds, typically a mix of domestic stock, international stock, and bond funds.

Sources indicate that the fund manager adjusts the allocation over time according to a schedule called a glide path. When you are decades away from retirement, the fund might hold 90% stocks and 10% bonds. As you get closer to your target year, that ratio shifts until the fund is much more conservative, sometimes holding more bonds than stocks by the time you retire.

Sources indicate that the glide path is simply the schedule that determines how the fund’s asset allocation changes over time. Think of it as the fund’s long-term plan for gradually reducing risk.

According to recent reports, different fund providers use different glide paths, and this matters more than most people realize. Some funds are more aggressive early on and pull back dramatically as retirement nears. Others maintain a higher stock allocation even into and through retirement, which some financial planners argue is actually smarter given how long retirement can last.

It has been revealed that the important thing to understand is that the glide path is not customized for you. It is a one-size-fits-all formula based on your expected retirement year, nothing more. Your actual risk tolerance, health, spending prepares, and other income sources are not factored in at all.

The biggest selling point is that target date funds require almost no ongoing attention. You pick one fund, contribute regularly, and walk away. For someone who has no interest in managing their investments, that convenience is genuinely valuable.

Sources indicate that because target date funds hold a mix of stock and bond funds, you get broad diversification across asset classes in a single investment. You are not putting all your money into a single sector or firm.

In a recent development, over time, a portfolio can drift away from its intended allocation as different assets grow at different rates. Target date funds handle this automatically, which is one less thing you have to manage yourself.

Target date funds are not without their drawbacks, and for many investors, those drawbacks are significant enough to look for a better option.

In a recent development, because target date funds are funds of funds, they often carry two layers of fees: the expense ratio of the target date fund itself and the underlying expense ratios of the funds it holds. Even a seemingly small difference in fees can cost you tens of thousands of dollars over a long investing career. Low-cost index funds, by comparison, often charge a fraction of what target date funds do.

It has been revealed that the glide path in a target-date fund is designed for the average investor retiring in a given year. But your situation is not average. You might have a pension, a working spouse, rental income, or a much higher risk tolerance than the fund assumes. None of that is reflected in how the fund manages your money.

According to recent reports, when you hand everything over to a target date fund, you give up control over your allocation. If the fund has a heavy position in international stocks or bonds that you would rather avoid, there is not much you can do about it while staying in the fund.

Variable quality across providers.

In a recent development, not all target date funds are created equal. The same target year fund from two different providers can have very different allocations, fee structures, and underlying holdings. Without digging into the details, it is easy to end up in a fund that does not match your actual needs.

It has been revealed that this is where the comparison gets important. A target date fund is actively managed in the sense that a team of people decides how to allocate and rebalance it over time. An index fund, on the other hand, simply tracks a market index like the S&P 500. There is no active management involved, which is exactly why the fees are so much lower.

In a recent development, decades of research consistently show that most actively managed funds underperform their benchmark index after fees. Target date funds are not immune to this problem. When you account for layered costs, many target-date funds trail what you would earn by simply holding a low-cost index fund over the same period.

A simple alternative that many investors use is called a three-fund portfolio: a U.S. total market index fund, an international index fund, and a bond index fund. You set your own allocation based on your age and risk tolerance, rebalance once a year, and pay minimal fees. It takes about 30 minutes a year to manage.

According to recent reports, this approach gives you the same diversification as a target-date fund, with far more control and significantly lower costs. And as a general rule, the more of your return you keep rather than paying in fees, the better off you will be over time.

Target date funds are not the right choice for every investor, but there are situations where they make sense.

Even in these cases, it is worth checking the expense ratio. If your plan offers a target-date fund with an expense ratio above 0.50%, consider whether there are lower-cost index fund options within the same plan.

It has been revealed that target date funds solve a real problem: they make it easy for people who do not want to think about investing to still participate in the market. That convenience has real value.

Sources indicate that but for investors who are willing to learn even a little bit about how to manage their own allocation, a portfolio of low-cost index funds will almost always be the better long-term choice. The fees are lower, the control is greater, and the returns tend to be better over time.

Sources indicate that if you are currently in a target date fund, that is not necessarily a problem. But it is worth understanding what you are paying and whether a simpler, lower-cost approach might serve you better. Investing at least 10% of your gross income is the priority. Where exactly that money goes is the next question worth asking.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives.
  • In a recent development, A health sharing blueprint (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance firm.
  • Tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives. Health sharing prepares have moved from a faith-based niche into a mainstream budgeting conversation. But before you switch, it’s worth understanding exactly what you’re trading away, not just what you’re saving.

In a recent development, A health sharing blueprint (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance firm. There’s no insurance contract, and no company is legally on the hook to pay your claims.

Tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed. Michigan’s insurance regulator adds that HCSMs aren’t classified as insurance because they don’t assume risk and have no legal obligation to pay members’ costs.

Example: Zion HealthShare is a modern health sharing community that markets itself as a lower-cost alternative to ACA intends, with no provider networks and members paying an “Initial Unshareable Amount” (their version of a deductible) before larger bills become eligible for sharing.

Read our review of Zion HealthShare.

Recent findings suggest that traditional health insurance is a regulated contract, an ACA marketplace initiative, an employer plan, or a private major-medical policy. The insurer must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one, and include the ACA’s essential health benefits (preventive care, maternity, mental health, and more), a distinction healthinsurance.org explains in detail when comparing HCSMs with ACA-compliant coverage.

Industry observers note that solo Health is another option built for self-employed people. It’s a self-funded major medical health initiative with a nationwide PPO network, and it works differently from both health sharing and ACA Marketplace coverage. Eligibility is based on a short health questionnaire. Read our full Solo Health review.

Industry observers note that employer-sponsored family premiums averaged $26,993 in 2025, and many 2026 ACA marketplace intends are seeing median premium hikes of 18–20% as subsidies shrink and medical costs climb. By comparison, health sharing contributions often run $150–$400 per person per month, roughly 30–50% less.

But that gap exists because health sharing prepares aren’t required to guarantee anything. Traditional insurers already deny 19–20% of claims on average (some carriers reportedly higher), so even “real” insurance isn’t friction-free, but at least it comes with legal appeal rights and state oversight. A health share’s review process is informal and ministry-specific, with no equivalent legal backstop if a bill gets rejected.

Recent findings suggest that it works best for generally healthy families who don’t qualify for meaningful ACA subsidies, are comfortable handling more paperwork and negotiating bills themselves, and want lower fixed monthly costs in exchange for taking on more risk. It’s a weaker fit for anyone managing a chronic condition, planning a pregnancy, or who needs the legal certainty of a regulated contract.

Health sharing can meaningfully lower your monthly healthcare costs, but the trade-off is real: you’re giving up the legal guarantee, essential-benefit mandates, and regulatory protection that come with traditional insurance. For a healthy family stretched thin by rising ACA premiums, it can be a reasonable bridge option. For anyone with ongoing medical needs, the savings usually aren’t worth the uncertainty.

Is a health sharing plan the same as a health insurance policy?No. It’s a voluntary cost-sharing arrangement, not a legally binding insurance contract.

Can I use a health sharing proposal and still contribute to an HSA?Not based on the health share alone; you also need to be enrolled in a genuine HDHP to be HSA-eligible.

Will a health sharing plan cover a pre-existing condition?Usually only after a waiting period, which varies by organization, often 12 to 36 months.

Does the ACA’s individual mandate penalty apply if I only have a health share?No, the federal individual mandate penalty was eliminated starting in 2019, so this isn’t a factor either way.

It has been revealed that having more than one type of debt is common, and that’s especially true once you graduate from college and start your first “real job.” You may have credit card debt, an auto loan, and a mortgage payment to make once you buy your first home. It’s also common to have other random debts to cover, including student loans.

If you’re like many who took out loans during college, you will likely be paying them off after you graduate. In fact, 82% of students who borrowed loans expect to be making payments post-graduation, according to a recent College Ave Student Loans survey.

That noted, you’ll want to make sure you’re balancing debt repayment with your savings goals along the way.

You’ll also want to make sure you’re paying down debts in the optimal order, or in a way that will help you save the most money on interest as possible while aligning with your goals. Which debts should you pay off first? Here’s a rundown of how to get the best results:.

Industry observers note that no matter which types of debt you have, credit card debt should be your first priority. Why? Because credit card debt is likely the most expensive debt you have by far.

Federal Reserve data highlights the average credit card interest rate on accounts assessed interest came in at around 22% as of May 2023, yet your credit card could easily be charging higher rates than the average.

To save as much money as possible, you should strive to pay as much as you can toward high-interest credit card bills each month. You can also pay down credit card debt faster with the help of a debt consolidation loan or a 0% APR balance transfer credit card.

According to recent reports, other unsecured debts like personal loan debt should come next in the debt payoff pecking order. After all, unsecured debts tend to have higher interest rates than secured debts like auto loans. In fact, the Federal Reserve also reported that the average interest rate on a 24-month personal loan came in at 11.48% as of May 2023, compared to the average rate of 7.81% on a 60-month auto loan.

Ideally, you’ll start paying more toward personal loan debt and other unsecured debts after all credit card debt is entirely paid off, although you should make at least the minimum payment on all your bills throughout the entire process.

It has been revealed that the next debt you’ll want to tackle is your student loans. I suggest focusing on these loans after other unsecured debts, since federal student loans (and many private student loans) come with low fixed interest rates and monthly payments that will not change over time. If you have federal student loans, you may even want to look into income-driven repayment plans.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re hoping to pay down student loans faster or just want to save money on interest, you can also consider refinancing your student loans to get a shorter repayment timeline, a lower monthly payment, or both. Just remember that refinancing federal student loans can mean losing access to income-driven repayment aims and federal protections like deferment and forbearance.

Once you have paid off or substantially paid down all your other debts, you can focus your efforts on secured debts you have like mortgage loans and auto loans. These debts should be dealt with last since they are secured with collateral and tend to offer lower interest rates as a result. For example, you can consider paying more than the minimum on your mortgage, a car loan, or both until they’re paid off completely.

Sources indicate that then again, you may want to pay off debts with extremely low interest rates as slowly as possible to free up more cash flow for living expenses and investments. If you took out a mortgage in January of 2021 when the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed rate home loan was as low as 2.65%, for example, it makes sense to make the minimum payment on that debt and invest your extra cash instead.

It’s important to make sure you balance debt repayment with other financial considerations. After all, focusing too much on debt repayment early in life can leave you behind when it comes to investing for retirement or saving up for a first home.

While you’ll want to eliminate credit card debt and other high-interest debts as promptly as you can, even if you have to stop saving and investing for a while, you can pay down student loan debt and secured debts at a slower pace while saving and investing for the future along the way.

Recent findings suggest that finally, make sure you have adequate emergency savings throughout your entire debt payoff journey, or that you begin saving for emergencies as soon as you can. Without a fully funded emergency fund, you can end up relying on credit cards and other loans to get by and ruin your debt payoff progress in the process.

How much should you save? While most experts recommend having an emergency fund that can cover three to six months of expenses, it’s okay to start small if you have to.

Having more than one type of debt is how it works for most people, especially when you’re young and in the early stages of your career. When it comes to paying it off, however, you’ll want to make sure you have a concrete strategy that can help you reduce interest charges and get where you want to be.

Focusing on credit card debt and other unsecured debts first always makes sense, since these debts aren’t secured by an asset and tend to charge much higher interest rates. You can focus on student loans next, followed by other secured debts you have like a home loan or car loan.

In the meantime, make sure you have an adequate emergency fund and invest in it for retirement. After all, debt won’t last forever if you’re serious about repayment, and saving and investing early can help you benefit from compound interest and avoid using credit cards for surprise expenses. Creating a budget to track these factors is your best bet.

If you need help creating one, or simply don’t know where to start, use this budget worksheet as your guide – you’ll reach financial freedom in no time.

That self-funded strategy pays eligible medical claims under the terms of your plan documents.

According to recent reports, of U.S. startups that raised early-stage venture capital from 1985 to 2009, about 55% ended at a loss for their investors, Harvard Business School researchers found. The 6% that returned more than five times the money brought in about half of everything investors got back.

Venture funds typically run at least 10 years and then cash out, the SEC notes, so expect pressure to grow fast enough to sell or go public before then.

Give each goal you’re saving for its own high-yield savings account or a named bucket inside one. That usually means one for yearly costs and one for your next major purchase, with your emergency fund in an account by itself. Separate balances show what each dollar is for, so you won’t spend one goal’s money on another by mistake.

Recent findings suggest that with all your savings in one account, a $9,000 balance looks like room for a vacation, even when $6,000 of it is your emergency fund. Nothing in your banking app says which dollars are already spoken for.

A goal needs its own account once it has a price and a date in the next few years, such as a car next year or a vacation next summer. A separate balance then demonstrates exactly how much of the price you’ve saved. Yearly costs like insurance premiums and holiday gifts can share one account, or each can get its own bucket as a sinking fund, money saved for that one cost.

The emergency fund stays apart because it’s the one balance that must be there in full when something goes wrong, and it belongs at a different bank from your checking.

It has been revealed that more accounts stop helping once one would charge a monthly fee or require a minimum balance, or once you’d have more balances than you’ll check each month. Skip an account for any goal you aren’t saving toward yet.

Industry observers note that open the goal accounts at one high-yield savings bank that lets you add them free. Capital One lets you open a separate 360 Performance Savings account for each goal, with no monthly fee or minimum balance. Ally Bank lets you split one savings account into buckets, named sections of the same balance.

Nickname each account for its goal and give it an automatic transfer on payday, or split one transfer among your buckets. The $9,000 then becomes a $6,000 emergency fund, $1,800 for insurance premiums and holiday gifts, and $1,200 toward a vacation, so the vacation account indicates $1,200 to spend, not $9,000.

When the vacation is paid for, rename its account for your next goal instead of opening another.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the shopping that pays is shopping for someone else, as a grocery shopper on a delivery app, a personal shopper, or a mystery shopper, since cash back on your own purchases only lowers what you spend. Before you count an app’s payouts as income, subtract what your miles cost and the self-employment tax you’ll owe.

A shopper app lets you pick your orders and hours around a day job, and it highlights each order’s pay before you accept it.

It has been revealed that instacart pays per batch, its name for a job, based on the driving distance, item count, and expected shopping time, plus promotions when demand runs high and 100% of the tip. Shipt pays per order based on its own estimate of the time and effort, at least $16 an hour by that estimate, plus bonuses and tips. Taking longer than the estimate earns nothing extra. Both require a reliable car and treat you as an independent contractor, so no tax comes out of your pay.

Price each mile at the IRS’s standard mileage rate, which is also what you can deduct for each business mile. The IRS bases it on what it costs to own and run a car, not just gas. At an illustrative 75 cents a mile, an hour of work that pays $25 and takes 20 miles of driving leaves $10 after the car. Self-employment tax, due once your year’s profit reaches $400, takes about 14% of that $10, so you keep roughly $8.60 before income tax. Over a full week, counting the hours you wait between orders, the same math gives your real hourly pay.

Industry observers note that instacart never penalizes you for passing on a batch, so you can skip any whose miles would cost most of what it pays. Log every mile you drive for work, since the deduction lowers your income tax and self-employment tax.

Before you accept any order or assignment, subtract its miles, priced at the IRS rate, from what it pays, then set aside about 14% of the rest for self-employment tax.

My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

📅 16 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.
  • Recent findings suggest that but man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here.
  • In a recent development, I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

Recent findings suggest that but man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

In a recent development, I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

But a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,.

“But I’m still gonna keep fighting it!”.

Yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

One of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder. And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health company that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

In a recent development, long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

Another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

Industry observers note that so I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s new tech giant, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:.

The next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

According to recent reports, and wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

It’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

This is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

It turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

In many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

In a recent development, but there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Sources indicate that many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

While this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me).

In a recent development, distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

Industry observers note that and while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

Recent findings suggest that so I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty quickly in the past.

Recent findings suggest that but on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”.

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”.

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

In a recent development, since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a fresh, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term plans again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

So Why Doesn’t Everyone Do This?

When you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that states, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the issue, you’ll see this:.

Stuff you should do BEFORE trying TRT:.

Industry observers note that the modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Industry observers note that since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

Many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

It has been revealed that more modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

My hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

Recent findings suggest that and it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower.

The great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The company that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

Note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

Needs vs. Wants – Ask What Would Suffer If You Cut the Expense

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (492 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • To sort your budget into needs and wants, ask what would happen if each expense disappeared.
  • It has been revealed that sorting this way shows what you can cut without real harm.
  • It has been revealed that ask the question of every expense, and the needs come down to a short list: shelter, utilities, basic food, insurance, health care, the transportation and child care that let you work, and minimum debt payments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

To sort your budget into needs and wants, ask what would happen if each expense disappeared. If your health, safety, housing, or ability to earn would suffer, it’s a need. Everything else is a want, and so is whatever you pay above the basic version of a need.

It has been revealed that sorting this way shows what you can cut without real harm. It also settles a debate with a partner, or with yourself, over what’s essential, because the answer turns on what would suffer, not on how you feel about the bill.

It has been revealed that ask the question of every expense, and the needs come down to a short list: shelter, utilities, basic food, insurance, health care, the transportation and child care that let you work, and minimum debt payments. Those payments make the list because a missed one hurts your credit and often adds a late fee, and falling behind on a car loan or mortgage can cost you the car or the home.

Much of what you can cut sits inside those needs. A phone and a reliable car both pass the test, but the newest phone and a new car are needs bought at a want’s price. The basic version is the need, and anything you pay above it is a want.

Recent findings suggest that say your phone bill covers unlimited data and the payment on a latest phone, for $95 a month, and a basic proposal with enough data to stay reachable for work would cost $30. The $30 is a need, and the other $65 is a want. Food splits the same way, with groceries as the need and whatever takeout costs beyond the same meals cooked at home as the want.

In a recent development, sort every charge on last month’s bank and card statements into needs and wants, splitting any that mix the two, then total each side. Compared with the 50/30/20 rule, the two totals show whether needs or wants are the reason your savings come up short.

When money gets tight, cut from the want side first, starting with whatever you’d miss least. Then trim each need to its basic version rather than dropping it. For the phone, that means switching to a cheap cell phone plan and keeping the phone you have long after its last payment.

Compare the best budgeting apps to find one that tracks each month’s charges for you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, before you buy a vacation home to rent by the night, base your math on how often similar rentals nearby are booked over a full year, not a seller’s projection or the peak season. Make the offer only if local rules allow nightly rentals and the home profits after cleaning, platform fees, insurance, taxes, and any manager’s cut.

Unlike a long-term rental, a vacation rental earns only on the nights guests book, while its mortgage, property tax, and insurance come due either way.

Take a cabin that rents for $230 a night and costs $19,000 a year for its mortgage, property tax, insurance, utilities, and upkeep. Each booked night adds $40 for cleaning, supplies, and booking platform fees, and a manager takes 25% of revenue. At 70% occupancy, meaning guests book 70% of the year’s nights, the listing agent’s spreadsheet shows the cabin earning about $15,000 a year after costs. If it books 85% of its summer weekends but, like similar cabins nearby, only 35% of the year, it loses about $2,000 a year.

Don’t count on that loss to cut your tax bill. When guests stay seven days or fewer on average, the IRS’s passive-loss rules don’t count the home as a rental activity. Its losses, depreciation included, then lower the tax on your salary only if you materially participate, such as working on it over 100 hours a year and no fewer hours than anyone else, including a manager.

Before you make an offer, take four steps:.

Run the math at the market’s year-round occupancy and again 10 percentage points lower, and buy only a home that makes money at both.

See what similar listings in your market book and earn on AirDNA before you tour homes.

In a recent development, A campaign that misses its goal leaves you owing nothing, since no backer is charged and Kickstarter takes no fee. The risky campaign is the one that reaches a goal set too low.

According to recent reports, once a campaign is funded, Kickstarter’s terms require you to finish the project and deliver every reward as promised. If the rewards cost more to make and ship than the pledges bring in after fees, you pay the difference. Promise backers a delivery date with room for factory and shipping delays, too.

It has been revealed that add up what delivering every reward costs: your factory’s price for the smallest run it will make, packaging, and shipping to each backer, by country if you ship abroad. Then add Kickstarter’s 5% fee and payment processing, which on a U.S. project is 3% plus 30 cents for each pledge of $10 or more.

Sources indicate that say a board game designer’s printer quotes $14 a copy for 2,000 copies, and shipping averages $10 a backer. She sets a $30,000 goal and raises $41,000 from 900 backers. Fees take about $3,550 and shipping $9,000, together about 30% of what she raised. The $28,450 left pays for all 2,000 copies, with 1,100 to sell after the campaign.

It has been revealed that to reach a goal that covers every reward, line up backers before you launch. Collect email addresses, then send people to your project’s Kickstarter pre-launch page, which emails its followers when you go live. Kickstarter states that, on average, 32% of the people who follow a pre-launch page go on to pledge, against 17% of those who follow after launch.

Kickstarter locks the goal at launch, so get your factory’s and shipper’s quotes in writing before you set it.

Equity crowdfunding lets you sell a stake in your business to your own customers, raising up to $5 million in 12 months through an SEC-registered crowdfunding portal. Before you launch, budget for the portal’s fee, financial statements that anyone can read, and the yearly reports you’ll owe your upcoming investors.

Your customers don’t need to be wealthy to invest, so regulars and fans can become backers with a reason to send you business. Unlike backers of a preorder campaign, they get a financial stake, not a product.

Industry observers note that the catch is raising the money in public, often from hundreds of investors. Under the SEC’s Regulation Crowdfunding rules, your offering statement, called Form C, goes into a public SEC database with your financial statements. After the raise, you owe annual reports, filed there within 120 days of your fiscal year’s end and posted on your website, though they need no accountant’s review.

What you sell decides what you give up:.

Pick a portal, such as Wefunder or StartEngine, and price the raise. Wefunder keeps 7.9% of what you raise plus up to $1,000 a year, and StartEngine estimates the accountant’s review and legal paperwork at $4,000 to $10,000. You need that review to raise more than $124,000 and an audit above $618,000, though a first crowdfunding raise can use a review up to $1,235,000.

In a recent development, say a neighborhood brewery raises $400,000 from 1,100 customers, most investing a few hundred dollars, to open a second taproom. On Wefunder it pays $31,600 and needs a review, not an audit. The SEC lets you test interest before you file if you say no money is being accepted and no one is committed, so poll your customers before you hire an accountant.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that FDIC insurance covers your checking, savings, CDs, and other deposits at an insured bank, up to $250,000 per ownership category, such as single or joint accounts.
  • A bank with the FDIC sign at its teller windows can still hold some of your money that the FDIC won’t cover.
  • Recent findings suggest that deposits are insured automatically, with nothing to apply for.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that FDIC insurance covers your checking, savings, CDs, and other deposits at an insured bank, up to $250,000 per ownership category, such as single or joint accounts. It doesn’t cover stocks, mutual funds, annuities, or crypto, even when you buy them at the bank. Confirm your bank on the FDIC’s BankFind, then total each category in its EDIE estimator.

A bank with the FDIC sign at its teller windows can still hold some of your money that the FDIC won’t cover. The branch that opens your savings account may also sell you an annuity, and a CD you open later can push your total past the limit.

Recent findings suggest that deposits are insured automatically, with nothing to apply for. But the FDIC doesn’t cover bonds, life insurance, or the contents of a safe deposit box. A money market deposit account counts as a deposit, while a money market fund, despite the similar name, is an investment with no FDIC coverage.

An ownership category is the way you own an account. The common ones are single accounts in your name alone, joint accounts, retirement accounts such as IRAs, and trust accounts, which include a savings account or CD naming a beneficiary to inherit it. Each category is insured on its own, but all your accounts in one category at one bank share one limit, whether they’re checking, savings, or CDs. Opening one at another branch of the same bank doesn’t change that.

Industry observers note that take a saver with two accounts at one bank, both in her name alone with no beneficiary. Her savings account holds $180,000, and her CD holds $90,000. Both are single accounts, so the FDIC adds them together, and her $270,000 is $20,000 over the limit. She could name a beneficiary on the CD, which would make it a trust account with its own limit, or move $20,000 to a different insured bank.

Industry observers note that to check your own coverage, search the FDIC’s BankFind by your bank’s name or web address to confirm it’s insured. Then enter each account’s balance and owners in EDIE, the FDIC’s Electronic Deposit Insurance Estimator, which indicates what’s insured at that bank and any amount over the limit. For a money app that isn’t a bank, look up the bank behind it instead.

Leave room under each category’s limit for at least a year of interest, since interest counts toward the limit through the day a bank fails.
