💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the world of very early retirement, we tend to ignore one of the most important things for normal retirees: the Social Security program.
  • Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great thing for the 73 million people who at the moment draw benefits, and it provides an essential safety net for many who don’t have much income from anywhere else.
  • But for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the world of very early retirement, we tend to ignore one of the most important things for normal retirees: the Social Security program.

Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great thing for the 73 million people who at the moment draw benefits, and it provides an essential safety net for many who don’t have much income from anywhere else.

But for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future. We aren’t thinking about money that eases us into our Golden Years, we need something that starts working now. Plus we’d rather not rely on our government keeping its promises that far into the future.

Those were my thoughts in 2005, when I was just a young retiree myself. But a funny thing happens when time passes: you get older. And you realize that there are plenty of other older people around too. And suddenly, Social Security is an important subject after all, that many people would like to know more about. But there is an endless pile of conflicting opinions:.

But when I did the math on all of this, I realized that it’s more confusing than it needs to be. Because when it comes to deciding on how Social Security fits into your retirement strategy, it really boils down to only one number:.

The Net Present Value of your future lifetime stream of Social Security payments.

In a recent development, that little piece of math jargon might not mean much if you don’t have fond memories of  Economics 101 class. But don’t worry, it’s easy to understand if you think of these two extremes:.

Sources indicate that if you want to retire in your 30s like I did, the value of your future Social Security is pretty close to zero. Even if the government keeps all of its promises, those payments are so far in the future that you need to save a full retirement ‘stash to get through the three decades until it kicks in.

On the other hand, if you’re already over 60 years old, contributed to Social Security throughout your long career and have a low cost of living, you may be eligible for payments that already meet all your needs.

In this situation, you are set for life. Social Security will in theory cover all your needs and rise automatically with inflation, so you don’t have to save any additional money.

In a recent development, in between these two extremes, the math gets interesting. Because while most people assume Social Security is useless until you reach full eligibility, the real story is that you can think of it as a chunk of money that you already have right now, which reduces the amount of saving you have to do on your own.

And there’s an easy way to calculate it, with an extremely useful thing called the Net Present Value calculation.

There’s an actual formula for this, but don’t worry you don’t have to memorize it because you can just have any Internet calculator, AI tool or spreadsheet do the math for you.

First let’s calculate the value a young couple might get if they do this calculation at 30 years old. We just have to make a few assumptions to have numbers plug into the formula:.

In a recent development, when you plug in all the numbers and calculate this (the Net Present Value of a 30 year stream of income), the first number you’ll get is $667,166. But that’s not the final answer – that is how much you’d need if you wanted the payments to start right now.

The final step is applying a simpler version of the formula a second time, to account for the fact that you don’t need the money until 32 years from now:.

At that point, you end up with a number around $98,280. But what does this mean?

It means that if you stuck $98k into an investment account today and let it compound for 32 years, at that point it would be big enough to provide a stream of $4000 payments for the following 30 years. And this even takes future inflation into account!It also means that the 30 year old retirees can mark an imaginary $98k onto their “net worth” spreadsheet and save that much less. Or at least think of it as a nice safety margin.

If you’re newly introduced to money and math, that may sound like sorcery, but if you’ve been investing for long enough you will understand that it really does work that way. So let’s re-run the example for a couple who is already 62 years old, and needs a $5000 income starting right now, that still needs to last 30 years.

That NPV calculation looks like this:.

And the answer is right around $834,000.

What this means, is that if they invested $834,000 into a fund that paid out 6% per year for 30 years before running dry, they’d get that exact same $5000 monthly income. And it would keep up with inflation.

Now that we’ve seen these examples from the extreme ends of the spectrum, we can see how this applies in a more typical situation. Here’s one that is loosely based on one from a real person I worked with last year:.

Sources indicate that shane Survivor is 55 and he has been through some hard times. He lost most of his savings in a business blowup a few years back, but really wishes he could still retire soon. His financial picture:.

In a recent development, most financial advisors would tell him to tough it out and  just keep working until he hits Social Security eligibility. At least 62 to get the minimum benefits, but maybe even longer to get to Full Retirement Age (67) or even until 70 to get the maximum benefit.

But wait! Let’s do the math because who wants to work another fifteen years when you’re already tired of working at 55!

Recent findings suggest that shane logs into the Social Security website SSA.gov and uses the online tool to calculate what his payout will be. I just did this myself so we can use my numbers:.

Let’s start by calculating the Net Present Value of each of these three options for our 55-year old friend:.

Industry observers note that whoa wait a minute, that’s a counterintuitive result! Am I really telling you that it’s actually less valuable to work longer so you can get the higher benefits? The answer is yes, for people who understand the concepts of “investing” and “the time value of money”.

According to recent reports, to really understand this, just imagine what would happen if you started taking those payments as early as possible (age 62) and tossed them into an index fund, earning 6% after inflation on average. After the first year, you’d already have about $24,300 and you’d still be piling in that extra two grand per month and the whole snowball would be starting to compound.

By the time your more patient friends started drawing $2796 payments five years later, you’d already have over $137,000. It’s such a big lead that the 67-year-old will never catch up.

But let’s go back to Shane’s real situation and see if he can retire:.

Industry observers note that so the answer is no, not quite yet. But he’s closer than it looks: every year of additional work will have a triple effect because it will:.

As soon as his combined ‘stash investment income plus the Social Security payment reach $3000 per month, he’s done.

Industry observers note that and of course, any additional tricks he can apply like streamlining his spending and boosting his income, will make this even faster. I’d give him about three years before reaching liftoff.

So how can YOU use this information to speed up your own retirement?

It has been revealed that the net effect of Social Security is that it should help you worry a little less and work a little less. The worrying part should benefit everyone, and the working part is kind of a sliding scale:.

For example as a 51-year-old, I can look at my number of roughly $350,000 and say yeah, that’s quite a major boost – enough to buy an entire house in many areas of the country or enough to fund multiple lifetimes of high-end groceries. And until now I had never even considered it as part of my retirement savings!

Frequently Asked (or Complained) Questions.

Now that we’ve covered the facts, I can already hear the complaints coming.

What if Social Security is canceled or greatly reduced by the time I reach that age?

Yeah, it might happen, but it’s also a top priority for most voters in our aging population. So it’s hard for politicians to make cuts. What is more likely is that the benefits will be cut for wealthier people. And if you find yourself in that camp (as I do), you won’t actually need the payments.

According to recent reports, sure, it’s not “fair”, but you know what? I can think of more fun ways to enjoy the fact that I’m a rich person rather than complaining about how some government program is “unfair”, and so can you.

Nobody can live on just a Social Security check!

First of all, millions of people do. In fact, last time I checked my own annual spending it was under $30k, most of it on optional luxuries, which is less than my expected payout!

But more importantly, most of us won’t have to, because we are also investing healthy sums on our own.

I’m still scared and worried about something else!

Recent findings suggest that now this is the root of the issue. In fact, worry is the root of almost all concerns. And so that’s what we need to focus on in our future work. For some reason, I have managed to live the last twenty years pretty much completely free from financial worries, and I had assumed everyone else was the same way. But it turns out this is not the case, even among people much wealthier and more advantaged than I am.

So in the next article, we need to get into that.

Bonus Materials: the Quirk of Social Security Contributions.

Industry observers note that to illustrate this point, I ran a simulation of two people who each make a $100k salary and contribute accordingly, but one retires after 10 years and that poor second guy works the full 35. Look at the difference in their benefits:.

Industry observers note that so the early retiree only worked and contributed about 28% as much as the late retiree. But his benefits are still a much higher 45% of the significant earner’s payouts. In summary? Social Security provides a mild incentive for slacking.

Sources indicate that one other factor: after retiring earlier, you might still end up contributing more than you think. This is because any income you earn later in life through optional employment (or self employment) will trigger more contributions. In my 21 years of retirement, I have ended up earning and contributing more during about 15 of those years, bringing my average level up much higher than I originally expected.

Final Tip: If in doubt, ask your Favorite AI.

Here are the eight, from the friendliest return terms to the costliest:.

In a recent development, the sellers with free mail returns make it cheap to order two sizes and keep one. Say you’re between a 10 and a 10.5 in a $140 running shoe from Running Warehouse. You pay $280 up front, $140 comes back once the refund posts, and the return costs nothing. From a seller that deducts $9.95 by mail, the same order at the same price leaves the pair you keep costing $149.95.

Sources indicate that keep any try-on indoors, since most of these sellers refund only unworn pairs. Zappos also wants its shoe box back without tape or postal labels, so pack it inside a shipping box.

It has been revealed that buy a size you’re unsure of from Zappos, Running Warehouse, or Nike as a member, or from DSW, Famous Footwear, or Nordstrom Rack when one of their stores is near you. Save 6pm and Joe’s New Balance Outlet for a model you already own in the right size.

If a bank turned your business down, apply for an SBA microloan of up to $50,000 from a nonprofit lender on the SBA’s list of microlenders. These lenders also coach borrowers on marketing and management. The money can buy equipment, inventory, or supplies, but it can’t pay off debt or buy real estate.

Industry observers note that the SBA funds these lenders but doesn’t review your credit. Each lender decides who qualifies and sets your rate and terms.

A microloan tops out at $50,000, carries a fixed rate, and must be repaid within seven years. The SBA notes rates usually run 8% to 13%. The business can be brand newly introduced, but it must be a for-profit small business in the U.S. Since April 2026, an SBA policy also requires every owner to be a U.S. citizen or national whose main home is in the U.S., which rules out green card holders.

Sources indicate that SBA rules let a lender go past $20,000 only after you show that the business can’t get credit elsewhere at a comparable rate and that it’s likely to succeed. A bank’s rejection in writing helps you show the first.

The money can also serve as working capital, the cash that runs the business day to day, or pay for furniture, fixtures, and machinery.

Say a mobile dog groomer turned down by her bank borrows $18,000 at a fixed 9% over five years to outfit a van. Her payment would be about $374 a month, and she’d pay about $4,420 in interest over the loan.

According to recent reports, the coaching can start before you borrow. Lenders can spend up to half of their SBA coaching grants on people who haven’t borrowed yet.

It has been revealed that find lenders on the SBA’s list of microlenders, filtered to your state, and call two or three for help with your application. Ask each for its rate, what property it would hold as collateral, and whether you’d sign a personal guarantee, which makes you personally responsible for the loan.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when the Federal Reserve raises rates, the variable rates on your credit card balances and home equity line of credit climb on their own, but your savings rate rises only if your bank raises it. Put extra payments toward those balances first, and move the cash you’re saving to a high-yield savings account that passes the increase on.

The Fed raised its benchmark rate a quarter point in September, its first increase since July 2023.

Sources indicate that A variable rate on a credit card or a home equity line of credit (HELOC) follows an index such as the prime rate, which moves with the Fed’s rate. Card issuers normally can’t raise the rate on a balance you already owe, but a rise in that index is one of the exceptions, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes. On a $10,000 card balance carried all year, each percentage point added to the rate costs about $100 in interest.

In a recent development, online banks have passed more of each increase on to savers. During the 2022 and 2023 hikes, they raised deposit rates about 0.3 percentage point more than branch-based banks for each full point the Fed added, a National Bureau of Economic Research study found. At an online bank paying 4%, $20,000 earns about $800 a year. At a big bank paying 0.01%, it earns $2.

Pay down card balances first, then a HELOC ahead of any fixed-rate loan charging the same rate or less. A card balance you’ll carry for months can move to a fixed-rate personal loan, or to a 0% balance transfer card you can pay off before the 0% period ends, after you compare the fees. If you’ll borrow for a car or a home soon, lock in a fixed rate before you buy.

Recent findings suggest that keep your emergency fund in a high-yield savings account. For fresh certificates of deposit (CDs), stick to terms of a year or less until rates level off, or build a CD ladder so part of your money comes due every six months.

Cash beyond that fund belongs on any card balance you carry. Banks charged an average 22.36% on cards carrying a balance in the third quarter, the Federal Reserve reports, more than five times what a 4% savings account pays.

Startup pitch competitions award cash, feedback, and investor introductions without taking a share of your company. Enter contests limited to your industry, region, school, or stage of growth, where the field is small, and skip any whose prize isn’t worth the travel and weeks of preparation. Read the rules first, since a few prizes are investments that take equity.

Sources indicate that universities, cities, corporations, and conferences all run these contests. For a founder too early for a bank loan or an investor’s check, a well-chosen one is among the cheapest sources of money and feedback.

According to recent reports, your odds depend on who else can enter. A contest limited to your school, region, industry, or stage of growth draws from a smaller pool than one open to every startup. MIT’s $100K competition, for one, awards a $100,000 grand prize without taking a share of the company, and its rules admit only teams with a current MIT student.

It has been revealed that grow-NY, a food and agriculture contest in upstate Fresh York, shows what to look for in the rules. Its $1 million top prize comes in stages as the winner hits milestones. The winner gives Cornell University, which runs the contest, either a right to 3% of the tech giant or a promise of future shares. It must also locate or do business in the region for at least 12 months.

Then weigh each prize against what competing costs you: the entry fee, the travel, and the weeks you’ll spend on slides and practice instead of on customers.

Build the pitch around a clear problem, the customer who has it, and early proof that customers want what you sell, such as sales, a trial run, or a waitlist. Cut it to the time limit, look up who’s judging so you can lead with what they care about, and expect questions about your numbers.

Recent findings suggest that picture a student team that enters three regional contests in one spring. It loses the first, wins $15,000 in the second, and at the third meets an angel investor, someone who invests her own money in startups. A year later, she leads the team’s first funding round.

Win or lose, leave with the judges’ feedback and their contact information. Ask the organizer for your scores and the judges’ comments. Within two days, send each judge who asked a hard question a better answer and a short update on your progress.

#91028. SBA Loans Cost Less Than Online Business Loans – If You Can Wait Weeks

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

SBA Loans Cost Less Than Online Business Loans – If You Can Wait Weeks

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Choose an SBA loan over an online loan if you can wait weeks.
  • In a recent development, owners turn to online lenders for speed.
  • Small Business Administration guarantees up to 85% of most 7(a) loans, which banks and other approved lenders make.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Choose an SBA loan over an online loan if you can wait weeks. The SBA’s guarantee comes with a capped rate and terms up to 10 years for most uses, 25 for real estate. Expect to pledge collateral on loans over $50,000, sign a personal guarantee, and, as a startup, put in at least 10% of the cost.

In a recent development, owners turn to online lenders for speed. In the Federal Reserve’s 2025 Small Business Credit Survey, 60% of firms that borrowed from online lenders mentioned their borrowing costs ran higher than expected, against 32% of large-bank borrowers.

An SBA loan is slower and cheaper. The U.S. Small Business Administration guarantees up to 85% of most 7(a) loans, which banks and other approved lenders make. In return for that backing, SBA rules cap a variable rate at the banks’ benchmark prime rate, now 7.00%, plus 3 to 6.5 percentage points, depending on the loan’s size.

Recent findings suggest that say a landscaper owes $120,000 on online term loans repaid over two years at 30% interest, about $6,710 a month. A 10-year 7(a) loan at a fixed 11% cuts that to about $1,650. The longer term costs more interest in total, about $78,000 over 10 years against $41,000 on the online loans. Extra payments shrink that, and a 7(a) loan shorter than 15 years carries no prepayment fee.

It has been revealed that A 7(a) loan of up to $5 million can cover working capital, equipment, real estate, debt refinancing, or starting or buying a business. A 504 loan, made through a nonprofit Certified Development Firm, finances buildings, land, and long-lived machinery at a fixed rate. SBA microloans of up to $50,000 come from nonprofit lenders.

Under the SBA’s lending rules, every owner of 20% or more personally guarantees the whole loan, and a loan over $50,000 needs collateral, though a lender can’t refuse you for weak collateral alone. A business open a year or less must put in at least 10% of the total cost, and so must most buyers of a business.

Sources indicate that to get an SBA loan, start with a bank that knows your business, and ask whether it’s an SBA Preferred Lender, one allowed to approve loans without the SBA’s review, which can take up to 10 business days. Or describe your needs in the SBA’s Lender Match tool, which lists interested lenders two business days later.

Apply once you know a major cost is coming, and keep online loans for needs that can’t wait weeks.

Compare the best small business loans and SBA lenders to choose where to apply.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That remarked, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Sources indicate that fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like fresh credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most notable challenges for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

It has been revealed that most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

One step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you strategy to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

It has been revealed that your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That remarked, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Recent findings suggest that some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

Industry observers note that while secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

According to recent reports, many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”.

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

Sources indicate that in fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

Sources indicate that there are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

According to recent reports, of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an issue with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Industry observers note that either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

15 Cities Where Rent Still Covers a Rental’s Mortgage – Then Check Taxes & Insurance

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buy your next rental where rent is high against home prices.
  • That share, a year’s rent divided by the price, is the gross yield, and it decides whether rent can cover a mortgage.
  • Sources indicate that now figure the mortgage payment on each, with 25% down and a 30-year loan at 7%.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buy your next rental where rent is high against home prices. In 15 Midwest and Southern metros, a typical house rents for 7.4% to 11.2% of its value a year. Before you offer, check the city’s taxes, insurance, and vacancy, and what houses on that street actually rent for.

That share, a year’s rent divided by the price, is the gross yield, and it decides whether rent can cover a mortgage. In Zillow’s October 2026 figures, a typical house in the San Diego area rents for about 5% of its value a year, while one in the McAllen, Texas, area rents for 11.2%.

Sources indicate that now figure the mortgage payment on each, with 25% down and a 30-year loan at 7%. A typical McAllen-area house, worth $189,000, rents for about $1,760 a month, roughly $820 more than its $943 payment. A typical San Diego-area house, worth about $1 million, rents for about $4,130, about $860 short of its payment of nearly $5,000.

At those terms, the typical rent is higher than the mortgage payment in all 15 metros below, by about $270 a month in Little Rock up to about $820 in McAllen. That margin still has to pay the property taxes and insurance, plus the repairs, empty months, and management every landlord budgets for, so those costs decide whether a house makes money.

Sources indicate that since October 2023, typical rents have risen faster than typical home prices, so the yield on a typical U.S. house has climbed from 7.0% to 7.4%.

Each price, rent, and yield here covers a whole metro area and uses Zillow’s typical single-family home value and rent, the middle of each market. Every metro on the list passed six tests:.

Two substantial Texas metros fell short. San Antonio’s typical rent rose only 0.7% over the past year, and Census’s metro estimates put Dallas’s rental vacancy at 14.7% this summer, nearly twice the national rate.

Here they are, from the highest yield down, with each metro’s typical house value and monthly rent.

Property taxes come out of the rent every year, and several states on this list tax a rental more heavily than an owner’s home. Texas’s homestead exemptions, which shield part of a home’s value from tax, go only to an owner’s main home, so a rental in McAllen or El Paso is taxed on its full value, the state comptroller explains. Michigan charges a rental up to 18 mills, or $18 per $1,000 of taxable value, in school operating taxes that an owner’s home skips, according to its Treasury Department.

Industry observers note that in South Carolina, a rental is assessed at 6% of its value, against 4% for an owner’s home, and pays school operating taxes the owner’s home skips, as Richland County, home to Columbia, explains. Indiana caps a rental’s yearly property tax at 2% of its assessed value, against 1% for an owner’s home, according to the state’s Department of Local Government Finance.

Insurance is the other big cost that varies by state. In Insurance.com’s 2026 study of quoted rates for a standard policy with $300,000 of coverage on the house, Nebraska, Oklahoma, and Kansas averaged more than $5,000 a year, about twice the $2,872 national average. Texas averaged $4,582. Get a quote on a landlord policy for the exact house before you offer.

Recent findings suggest that landlord law matters as well. Oregon, Washington, and California cap yearly rent increases statewide, while 36 states bar their cities from adopting rent control at all, according to the National Apartment Association, a landlords’ trade group.

Industry observers note that every number above describes a whole metro, which mixes blocks where houses rent quickly with blocks where they sit empty. Before you offer, compare the rent the seller quotes with what similar houses nearby actually rent for. If you’re buying in another state, have a local agent or property manager pull those rents for you.

Start with the two or three metros whose typical prices fit your budget, and run one real listing in each through the mortgage test above, using its own tax bill and insurance quote.

Find Small Business Grants Close to Home – Not in Washington

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Look for small business grants close to home, from city and state economic development offices, utilities, corporations, and foundations.
  • A grant is the cheapest money a business can get, since you never repay it and no one takes a share of the manufacturer.
  • Small Business Administration “does not provide grants for starting and expanding a business,” according to its own grants page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Look for small business grants close to home, from city and state economic development offices, utilities, corporations, and foundations. The SBA gives no grants to start or expand a business, and federal grants for companies mostly fund research or exporting. Apply only where your business fits the grant’s purpose.

A grant is the cheapest money a business can get, since you never repay it and no one takes a share of the manufacturer.

Sources indicate that the U.S. Small Business Administration “does not provide grants for starting and expanding a business,” according to its own grants page. The federal grants a company can win go mostly to research, through the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) programs, and to exporters.

So for a shop, a restaurant, or a service business, the grants worth chasing are local.

In a recent development, take a bakery owner who searches the federal grant listings and finds research and export programs, nothing for a bakery. Her city’s economic development office runs a storefront program that pays back half the cost of exterior work, up to $10,000. She applies before hiring anyone, as the program requires, wins a grant, spends $16,000 on a newly introduced sign, awning, and lighting, and gets $8,000 back once the work is done.

Here’s where to look, starting close to home, with what each source pays for and who can apply.

A real government grant never charges you a fee. The Federal Trade Commission says no agency will reach out to demand that you pay for a grant, and it warns against paying any up-front fee.

It also warns against paying for a list of grants, since the complete list of federal grants on Grants.gov is free.

Check the sender, too. The SBA claims it writes only from email addresses ending in @sba.gov, and that anyone claiming to be the agency from another address should be reported as fraud.

Read what the grant pays for first, since many fund a single purpose. Philadelphia’s Storefront Improvement Program covers exterior work such as signs, awnings, lighting, and paint, and STEP money goes only to export activities the SBA approves.

Then check what you’d have to put in yourself. Philadelphia’s program pays back up to half the cost of approved work, so you cover at least half and pay the whole bill until the city reimburses you. USDA’s Value-Added Producer Grants require a dollar-for-dollar match.

Industry observers note that many grants also want a business that’s already running. STEP is for established small businesses, and the $25,000 Wells Fargo grants the Manhattan Chamber of Commerce offered in 2026 required two years in business.

The competition is steep. Boston’s storefront program says it lacks the money to give a grant to every eligible business, and Hiring Our Heroes names five winners a round. Winning takes an application that answers the funder’s scoring criteria point by point.

Start with one call to your city’s economic development office, and ask which grants it’s funding this year, what each one pays for, and how much of the cost you’d have to cover.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Teach full time for five school years in a row at a low-income school, and Teacher Loan Forgiveness can cancel up to $17,500 of your subsidized and unsubsidized federal loans, depending on your subject.
  • Sources indicate that the comparison starts with your subject, which sets the cap on Teacher Loan Forgiveness (TLF).
  • The catch is what TLF does to Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Teach full time for five school years in a row at a low-income school, and Teacher Loan Forgiveness can cancel up to $17,500 of your subsidized and unsubsidized federal loans, depending on your subject. But those years can’t also count toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness, which has no cap, so compare the two before you apply.

Sources indicate that the comparison starts with your subject, which sets the cap on Teacher Loan Forgiveness (TLF). Secondary math and science teachers and elementary or secondary special education teachers can get up to $17,500, and other teachers up to $5,000.

The catch is what TLF does to Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF). PSLF cancels whatever federal Direct Loan balance remains after 120 qualifying monthly payments, made over at least 10 years at a public school or another qualifying employer. Take TLF, and your payments from those five years stop counting toward PSLF, so you’d need 120 more.

According to recent reports, for a small balance, TLF beats waiting for PSLF. A high school math teacher who borrowed $16,000 can have what’s left canceled after year five, since it’s under her cap. A colleague who also teaches math prepares to stay in public schools and repay on an income-driven strategy, which sets payments by income. With $60,000 in loans, she’d get at most $17,500 from TLF and likely far more from PSLF at year 10, so she skips TLF.

Before you count on TLF, confirm three things:.

Sources indicate that with a balance under your cap, you can ask your loan servicer each year for a TLF forbearance, which pauses payments so you don’t pay down debt TLF would cancel. Interest still builds and can push your balance past the cap.

After year five, have your principal, superintendent, or HR office certify the Teacher Loan Forgiveness Application, then send it to your servicer, one form per servicer.

Before you choose, use StudentAid.gov’s Repayment Calculator to compare what you’d pay in total under each program, since TLF can’t be undone after it’s granted.

#91020. Borrowing From Family to Start a Business? Sign a Note First

Borrowing From Family to Start a Business? Sign a Note First

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (499 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before family lends you startup money, put the terms in a note you both sign: the amount, interest rate, payment schedule, and who repays it if the business closes.
  • A handshake leaves each of you free to remember a different deal, and the difference indicates up the first time a payment is late.
  • Recent findings suggest that start by agreeing that it’s a loan, repaid on a schedule.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before family lends you startup money, put the terms in a note you both sign: the amount, interest rate, payment schedule, and who repays it if the business closes. Set the rate at or above the applicable federal rate, a minimum the IRS publishes monthly, so no part of the loan counts as a gift.

A handshake leaves each of you free to remember a different deal, and the difference indicates up the first time a payment is late.

Recent findings suggest that start by agreeing that it’s a loan, repaid on a schedule. Money your parents don’t want back is a gift, and a parent who gives you more than the annual gift tax exclusion in one year files a gift tax return. If they want a share of the profits, it’s a stake, which makes them part owners who get nothing back if the business fails.

According to recent reports, if the loan charges less than the applicable federal rate (AFR), the IRS’s below-market loan rules can treat the interest your parents gave up as a gift from them. In some cases, the IRS also counts it as income they owe tax on.

In the note, formally a promissory note, two terms need the most thought. The first is whether you or your business owes it. Money lent to your limited liability company (LLC) is generally its debt, not yours, so your parents carry the risk if it closes. The second is what happens to the balance if the business closes, whether you keep paying from your own income, pause the payments, or your parents forgive the rest.

In a recent development, say a son borrows $20,000 from his parents for four years. The IRS’s mid-term rate applies to loans over three years and up to nine. Suppose that rate is just under 5% when he gets the money, so they charge 5%. Forty-eight automatic transfers of about $461 repay it with about $2,100 in interest, and no one has to bring up a payment at a holiday dinner.

Sources indicate that ask for no more than your parents could afford to give away, since a fresh business can close before it repays anyone. Then give them a few days to decide how to lend without losing money or the relationship.

Look up the AFR for the month you get the money, write a rate at least that high into the note, and set up the automatic transfer the day it arrives.

0% Intro Business Cards Beat Startup Loans – If You Clear the Balance in Time

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pay for startup equipment and inventory with a business credit card that charges 0% interest on purchases for a year or more.
  • Borrowing at 0% costs less than most startup loans.
  • The catch is that the debt is yours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pay for startup equipment and inventory with a business credit card that charges 0% interest on purchases for a year or more. Divide the balance by the number of months the 0% rate lasts, round up, and set that payment on autopay, so your card is paid off before its regular rate starts.

Borrowing at 0% costs less than most startup loans. A microloan through the U.S. Small Business Administration, for one, generally charges 8% to 13% interest, depending on the lender.

The catch is that the debt is yours. Small-business cards typically carry a personal guarantee, so you and the business both owe the balance, a Federal Reserve report to Congress found. When the business has little or no credit history, the issuer relies more on your personal credit.

The same report explains that the protections in the CARD Act, the 2009 federal law on credit card practices, apply to personal cards, not business cards. So your card’s own terms decide what a late payment costs. On U.S. Bank’s Business Shield, one late payment, or one that bounces, ends the 0% rate early.

Charge only purchases that will bring in money soon, like the equipment you’ll work with and inventory you’ll sell. Months of rent and other bills are a poor fit, since a slow launch may not earn enough to repay them before the 0% rate ends.

Recent findings suggest that the longer the 0% period, the smaller each monthly payment can be. Bank of America’s Platinum Plus business card gives 0% for 15 billing cycles on purchases when you apply online, then a variable rate of 14.99% to 25.99%. The 0% period starts when the account opens, so apply when you’re ready to buy.

In a recent development, then divide the balance by the number of months the 0% rate lasts, round up, and set that amount on autopay, the same plan that pays off a balance transfer in time. A photographer who charges $8,400 in cameras and lenses to a card with 0% for 15 months would pay $560 a month by that math. Rounding up to $600 clears it in 14 months, with a month to spare.

Set up that autopay the day the card arrives, so no payment comes in late while you’re busy launching.

From the best small-business credit cards, pick one whose 0% period is long enough for a payment your business can afford.

I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

Industry observers note that these popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

My goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:.

When it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

In a recent development, on the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

The most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

True Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

Sources indicate that one of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

According to recent reports, the program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

It has been revealed that another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

True Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

Industry observers note that financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

Dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

The cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive proposal for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

According to recent reports, while Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

Sources indicate that financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable plan to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

MoneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

One of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

Recent findings suggest that the teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

MoneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program also includes exercises like the transfer of ownership, which guides participants in acknowledging God’s ultimate ownership of their resources. These introspective activities can be powerful tools for reshaping participants’ mindsets and habits around money.

However, one potential drawback of MoneyLife is that its emphasis on biblical principles and spiritual practices may come at the expense of providing highly actionable, practical financial strategies.

In a recent development, moneyLife is ideal for Christians who are seeking a deeply biblical understanding of money management and are willing to engage in a more studious, reflective learning process. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. However, those primarily looking for a simple and easy financial strategy or a more interactive learning experience may find other programs that better fit their needs.

Having gone through all 3 programs, here is my personal experience and recommendations:.

Recent findings suggest that I can honestly say that True Financial Freedom was a life-changing experience. Bob and Linda’s warm, relatable teaching style made me feel like I was learning from trusted friends who truly cared about my success. The program’s emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy was a game-changer for me, as it helped me develop a proposal that fit my unique situation and goals.

Personally, True Financial Freedom struck that balance better than any of the other programs on the list and gave me the strategy to move forward. My savings, giving, and earning have all increased in significant ways since taking the program.

In a recent development, for those who are drowning in debt and need a clear, structured proposal to get out, I highly recommend Financial Peace University. Dave Ramsey’s no-nonsense approach and the step-by-step “Baby Steps” system can provide the motivation and direction needed to tackle debt head-on. The debt snowball method, in particular, has helped countless people experience quick wins and build momentum on their debt-free journey. Just be prepared for a more intense, boot camp-style learning environment.

If you’re seeking a program that deeply explores the biblical principles behind money management, Crown’s MoneyLife might be the right fit for you. The program’s emphasis on spiritual practices and aligning your finances with your faith can be incredibly powerful for those who want to grow in their understanding of God’s perspective on wealth. However, be prepared for a more academic, reading-intensive learning experience and less focus on highly practical, actionable strategies.

Ultimately, the best program for you will depend on your unique financial situation, learning style, and personal goals. If you’re looking for a grace-filled, practical approach that helps you thrive in God’s Kingdom while making an eternal impact, I highly recommend True Financial Freedom. If you need a structured, intensive plan to get out of debt fast, Financial Peace University could be your best bet. And if you desire a deep dive into the biblical foundations of money management, MoneyLife is worth considering.

In a recent development, regardless of which program you choose, the most key thing is to take action and invest in your financial education. By doing so, you’ll be better equipped to handle the resources God has entrusted to you and experience the joy and freedom that comes from aligning your finances with your faith.

Will the AI Bubble Destroy our Retirement?

📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a phrase we keep having to dust off and use again, as the years go by and the market keeps surprising us.
  • When it crashes, some of us worry because we see our retirement stash shrinking.
  • But even when it rises to record levels and then to super-duper-crazy record valuations, we find reason to worry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wow, how about that stock market?

It’s a phrase we keep having to dust off and use again, as the years go by and the market keeps surprising us.

When it crashes, some of us worry because we see our retirement stash shrinking.

But even when it rises to record levels and then to super-duper-crazy record valuations, we find reason to worry. Because that just means an even bigger crash is coming, right? Especially when this boom-bubble is built on the back of something as frenzied as the present Artificial Intelligence boom… right?

It has been revealed that for those who have been happily tuned out of this drama and just enjoying life: Congratulations! Keep up the great work. But just to give you a quick background for the purposes of this article, here’s the AI story in three points:.

Investors worry that while AI is definitely a major invention, the mania around it is still too much, too fast, and thus we are due for an even bigger version of the dot com crash we had in the early 2000s. Which happens to be an interesting subject for me, since that was the boom that boosted my own early career and got me on the path to early retirement … before the ensuing crash almost cost me my job and my citizenship application.

As an aging Internet Financial Guru, I have the privilege of getting lots of questions about this investment cycle, just as I have about past booms and busts. And to address them, I decided to not only write this blog article but also create a little talk about it – which I already gave for the first time at an event called Camp FI Midwest earlier this month. I also hope to polish it up and deliver an improved version at the Bogleheads conference in November.

Recent findings suggest that so what that means is that today you not only get a blog post, but a few silly presentation slides to go with it for extra entertainment. All with no need for a plane ticket or all that hassle of leaving your house. So let’s get into it!

Industry observers note that so I recently hit 21 years of retirement. This means I’ve grown pretty comfortable with the idea. But it still threw me for a loop one time when a friend asked me this question:.

“How can you be retired, and comfortable in your retirement, and sleep at night, with everything that’s going on in the world? Aren’t you worried?”.

And I was like, “No, what should I be worried about?”.

In a recent development, but if you’re a news watcher and a worrier yourself, you can probably think of a few things I should be worried about. Perhaps stuff like this:.

You’ve got our corrupt and/or dangerous politicians like Trump and Putin menacing the world. Inflation eroding our purchasing power, the AI Bubble, the towering US National Debt, the Iran war and the Ukraine war and all these other wars that are just on the verge of tipping us all into destruction.

But it turns out these were not the things my friend was asking about.

It has been revealed that because she actually asked me this question over twenty years ago… In the year 2006. So back then we were worried about entirely different things, right?

It has been revealed that back then we had corrupt and/or dangerous leaders like Bush, Hussein and of course Bin Laden. There was still a war in the middle east but it was Iraq instead of Iran. We were still worried about the National Debt and Inflation. And we also worried about our overvalued stock market. But back then it was because of the housing bubble instead of the AI bubble. And instead of AI taking our jobs it was going to be outsourcing to India and China.

Oh and here’s an interesting one: There was a big debate over Peak Oil, and whether the world was doomed because fossil fuel use was always increasing while supply was bound to decrease. And it turns out the opposite happened as you’ll see below.

So then after all this worry in 2006, what ended up happening?

Well we did get the Great Financial Crisis, which was caused by a combination of irrational exuberance over increasing house prices combined with a foolish degree of fancy leverage in the financial instruments used to issue mortgages. And it was the biggest crash since the Great Depression.

Sources indicate that but even in that craziest of situations, look how minor it looks in the big picture. A $100,000 investment still ended up ballooning into $852,000 today. And if you look carefully in here you can just see the Covid Crash tucked in there in 2020. Remember that?

And not only that, the rest of the world got a lot better too:.

In a recent development, the portion of people living in extreme poverty dropped from 20% in 2005 to only 8% over the next 20 years. Infant mortality – children who die in their first year of life – was cut in half. Clean energy became a thing as solar panels became about 40 times cheaper. So solar generation now makes up the vast majority of all the new generation we add today (the equivalent of 647 nuclear power plants of peak capacity added last year, but with much cheaper and easier solar panels). And sales of pure electric cars have gone from zero up to about a quarter of all the cars sold on Earth last year, on its way to 100%, which is where they already are in Norway.

So if we circle back to that question my friend asked me 20 years ago: do you think I should have focused my energy on worrying about an uncertain future, or optimism?

Which of course brings up the question: Is it different this time?

Recent findings suggest that maybe the US national debt is finally massive enough to really start messing with us. Maybe the AI bubble is way bigger than the housing bubble and we won’t bounce back from this next stock market crash. Or maybe AI will spin out of control into a super intelligence that takes over the planet and realizes it does not need us any more.

And the financial media loves to spin a good scary story about all of this. But you know what the fear mongers all seem to be missing?

It’s the fact that at the core, our prosperity does not come from the financial system or the stock market, which are just some made-up numbers on some computers.

Really, Prosperity comes from Productivity.

In a recent development, we first covered this lesson right here on MMM, in the 2014 Classic entitled, “Why we are not really all doomed”. And sure enough, twelve years later the timeless lessons therein remain just as true now as they were back then.

And the lesson is really simple: the world of capitalism is always choppy and prone to wild swings. But if you peek beneath the waves, there are real people in there, doing real work and coming up with real inventions.

In a recent development, in fact, the very idea of an “economy” or a financial system is just another human invention. If the whole system crashes because we don’t like the numbers we see in there, we can literally make up some newly introduced numbers and then get back to work. Which is exactly what we did in 2008 and many times before that, and it seems to have worked just fine.

Meanwhile, we still have every tool we ever invented to boost our productivity. And our standard of living, and our economic growth, and our possibility of retiring early, all come from high productivity.

But even Productivity and Prosperity aren’t all that important.

Sources indicate that because once we reach a certain standard of living, human happiness kind of tops out in that dimension. In first-world countries, we blew past those minimum requirements several decades ago. And then we start looking for other factors to maximize our overall happiness. All anybody really wants is to lead the happiest, most satisfying life they can manage.

And when you think of it that way, your wealth is really just part of your life situation, which is part of this little green slice of the happiness pie.

Genetics is unfortunately the biggest slice – some people are just plain happier than others. But there are also quite a few choices that are within your control.

Focusing on good close relationships and being kind to people. Practicing Gratitude and Optimism as your lifelong philosophy. And making sure you pack as many healthy (outdoor) activities into your days as you can.

So, I didn’t invent anything fresh in this blog post. And most of it is just a repackaging of the same stuff I’ve been writing about since 2011. And yet some regular MMM readers who presumably know all this stuff are STILL afraid. Afraid to retire, afraid of things in their unknown future. Can we fix this?

I think the biggest problem is Fear Itself.

Industry observers note that the problem is that as a Human Being, you are basically a Danger Detection Machine. And this pervasive background fear is just a trait we evolved to protect ourselves from danger.

According to recent reports, but there’s a weird thing about our detection machinery. We can adapt and learn to function even in very dangerous environments, but when the danger goes away, we keep looking for stuff to worry about. In other words, there is a problem with fear: for many of us, it never really goes away. It just keeps moving the goalposts.

While Nature has wisely endowed us with a fear of predators and disease, if you solve those things you’ll just start worrying about whether or not you can get enough food. And supplies, and protecting yourself against scarcity.

If you succeed, next you’ll be worrying about if you can fit in with your tribe, because if you don’t, you might be exiled.

And if you don’t have to worry about that, you’ll go back to worrying about money for different reasons. Thanks to our tendency to use comparisons rather than absolutes (sometimes called “anchoring bias” and the “contrast effect”) when judging our lives, just getting out of poverty isn’t enough. We just move on to wanting more money.

And then, when some people get enough money to have a comfortable upper-middle-class lifestyle, they take the logical next step of starting a Homeowner’s Association, so they can worry about the unauthorized weeds on their neighbor’s lawn. Or maybe a Political Action Committee in hopes of controlling the color of their future neighbors’ skin.

And even if all the lawns and gardens are green and perfect and people get really rich, they just move on to worry about tax strategy, leaving a huge inheritance for their children, and avoiding RMDs.

Required minimum Distributions. This is when, if you get to 75 years old and you have too much money, the government will start making you withdraw some of that money so you can spend it and pay taxes on it. And people actually worry about this. I shit you not.

In a recent development, but wait! You can actually fight back against fear. It’s just a bit tricky because it requires some self awareness. But you have the advantage, because you have the ability to think rationally. And your fear is quite clearly irrational.

And the first step is to understand your own history. Are you afraid of certain things because of your childhood?

Recent findings suggest that I might have been afraid of running out of money, because in my family there was always a perceived shortage of the stuff, possibly enforced by my Dad’s scarcity mentality. And he was aware that his own fears of scarcity came from childhood as well: he grew up in a truly low income family in the 1940s and 50s, under the care of parents who had lived through the Great Depression of the 1930s.

In a recent development, even more significant is that survivors of trauma and abuse will very likely end up with fear problems in adulthood. It’s natural, and unfortunately abuse is way more widespread even in this country than we would like to admit. This makes it harder to eliminate, but it still helps to understand that your past is what is causing these feelings, rather than an objective understanding of the present.

Identify the Fear: Once you understand yourself, it helps to talk through the nature of your fear in more detail. This is also often taught in therapy. What would happen if it really came true? What would the worst case scenario be? It’s often not all that bad.

In one post, why you’ll probably never run out of money, I went to great lengths to imagine what it would mean for a wealthy person like yourself to actually let the well run dry, and let’s say you’ll probably never come close.

Recent findings suggest that once you identify the fear, you can start taking action. And one of the best and most accurate slogans ever is that action cures fear. It’s because it makes the unfamiliar, familiar. And you get confidence that you can really create change. And then that learning creates Resilience – the ability to adapt to ANY fresh situation, which is a trait also known as Badassity. And with sufficient Badassity, nothing is scary.

Think about it: if you had the skills and abilities to handle ANY situation, skills in the mental and physical and even the realms of emotion and wisdom, would you really have to worry about anything?

It has been revealed that the next thing you can do is tune out all the unnecessary crap from your daily mental diet. And for most Americans, this means the daily news.

The news is not helping you to keep informed, it’s just poisoning your mind with a hand-picked selection of the scariest stories of each day. If you want to learn about something, go find a book on the subject. And if you want to make a difference, the only thing that counts is not the news stories you watch – it’s only the actions that you take – in other words, your Positive Behaviors.

Industry observers note that as a human being, you are wired to solve problems with both your body and your mind, and you are meant to do it outdoors. So if you spend all your days in a house and a car and in an office using the computer, of course you are going to have some mental health problems. This should not be a surprising thing you need to ask your therapist about, it is an expected result of not living the life that you were literally created to live as a Human being!

So you need to focus on learning, moving, and solving problems. And you need your food and drink intake to be in alignment with all of this too. Life will get a lot less scary as soon as you are living life in the way you were built to live it.

According to recent reports, then finally, you can start swapping out the fear-mongers in your life, for other positive, productive, optimistic people. And watch how much the positive mentality rubs off on you. In the FI community, at least the subgroup of people that I like to spend time with, nobody focuses on fear. It’s all just about living the best life we can, and helping other people do so as well.

In a recent development, so now that we know how to fight back against fear, we can start using a new approach when we go into anything new. And that approach is something I like to call Everything is an Experiment.

And this applies whether you are talking about something tiny like a new paint color. But it scales up to bigger things like switching to a new car, or a new house, meeting new friends, looking for new love by going through the sometimes hell of first dates, a new job, or even quitting your last job by taking an early retirement.

So let’s bring this back around to AI, the thing that everybody seems to be afraid of right now.

I think of our fresh AI era as just being another giant experiment. And because of this, I don’t find it even remotely scary. But I do find it endlessly fascinating.

In a recent development, first of all, it’s a change. A potentially unknown one, and for some people that’s scary.

Sources indicate that but instead of just leaving it there and then doom-scrolling ominous news articles about it, why not learn why people are so excited about AI? As someone with a lifelong background in technology and economics (and a general lack of political affiliation), I can see a lot more potential upside than downside. And that mainly comes from the fact that I see AI as just a very fancy form of Cognitive Nail Gun.

It will boost our efficiency, which means our productivity, which means prosperity. Because it’s really just a super smart brain that we all get to tap into at a fairly negligible cost.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, it will also displace workers like every other fresh productivity technology. It’s already doing so in things like entry level office jobs in software and finance. It will eventually replace car and truck drivers, and so on. But in exchange, these services will become cheaper, and new industries will be created because of the new technology. Much like the Internet itself, and then the enormous industries unleashed by smartphones and mobile apps.

In a recent development, and one unfortunate side effect of these new inventions is that they tend to concentrate their rewards on the people who own them. If you own a house building company and employ a bunch of carpenters and give nail guns to the best of those carpenters, you can now lay off the other half and still get more done. If you own a company and roll out AI to the workers, you can do the same thing.

It has been revealed that and if you’re a big public organization, your shareholders also benefit, which happens to include most of the people reading this. As you’ve seen when looking at your portfolios over the past two years.

Artificial Intelligence is just like any other fresh thing that pops into your life: it’s an opportunity to make some choices. And it is up to you to decide if this is something to be afraid of, or to use as a trigger for learning, action, and living a more interesting life.

So that’s my little talk (and surprisingly long blog post) on Fear versus the AI bubble.

I hope that if you do feel fearful about this or any other issue in your future life, you’ll take it as a cue to learn more about your own fear and emotions and manage them as the root cause they are, rather than just trying to avoid the symptoms. Because in the wise words of my friends The Donegans:.

Everything you want in life, that you don’t already have,lies on the other side of Fear. Because if you weren’t afraid to go out there and get it, you would already have it.

Startup Accelerators Cost You a Stake – Apply Only if You’ll Raise From Investors

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (496 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apply to a startup accelerator only if your business could grow fast enough to raise money from investors.
  • According to recent reports, at the best-known programs, the seed money is no grant.
  • Y Combinator’s standard deal puts $500,000 into each startup it accepts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apply to a startup accelerator only if your business could grow fast enough to raise money from investors. In exchange for a slice of your manufacturer, it usually gives you seed money, mentors, and introductions to investors. If you’ll never sell a stake, get free advice from SCORE or a Small Business Development Center instead.

According to recent reports, at the best-known programs, the seed money is no grant. Every dollar of it buys a piece of your organization.

Y Combinator’s standard deal puts $500,000 into each startup it accepts. Of that, $125,000 buys a fixed 7% of your company, and Y Combinator invests the other $375,000 through a SAFE, a contract that turns into shares when investors later buy your stock at a set price. Techstars takes a fixed 5% for $20,000 and, in most programs, puts another $200,000 into the same kind of SAFE. Either way, the program’s stake grows past its fixed 7% or 5% once its SAFE turns into shares.

It has been revealed that along with the cash, that stake gets you mentors and introductions to investors. Many programs end with a demo day, where you pitch your tech giant to investors. That trade is worth making only if you’ll go on to raise money from angel investors or venture capital firms. A two-founder software startup that gives up a fixed 7%, then raises its first round from investors it met at demo day, gets what it paid for.

A business that won’t raise from investors should look for help that costs no stake. Universities, cities, and companies run incubators that can offer workspace and advice. Some are free, while others charge a fee or take a stake, so ask first. A bakery that rents low-cost kitchen space from a city incubator and gets coaching there keeps the whole business. SCORE’s mentors advise U.S. business owners for free, and Small Business Development Centers offer no-cost consulting.

According to recent reports, for a startup that will raise money, judge a program by its people and its terms. Find out which investors come to its demo day and whether its mentors have built companies like yours. Read the terms of both the fixed stake and the SAFE, and check whether you must move, since Y Combinator’s three-month program meets in person in San Francisco.

Before you apply, ask each program what share of the companies in its last two classes raised money within a year of demo day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the three-man Russian team returned to Everest’s West Ridge but found the route even more difficult than they expected. After two days of struggle, they’re heading back to Base Camp.

According to recent reports, on October 20, Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov went back up to the Lho La and pitched their tent on the wide plateau beyond. They still had time to fix more rope higher up.

“We moved…over terrain we’d already covered on the previous rotation,” the climbers texted to team member Natalya Belyankina, who had to abandon the expedition due to illness.

“The weather is good: sunny, with light winds, but cold,” they noted. “Progress was painfully slow today due to heavy packs and a persistent cough,” the climbers noted later.

It has been revealed that on Wednesday, they hoped to reach 7,500m, spend the night there, check the route ahead, and then retreat to the plateau. However, they didn’t get as far as they had planned.

According to recent reports, “We didn’t cover much ground today,” leader Andrei Vsiliev texted Anna Piunova of The Mountain Club. “The route is no walk in the park. We have to climb steep snowy slopes that conceal rock sections underneath.”.

Industry observers note that to make things worse, they found no suitable bivy spots at their highest point, so they had to retreat to a place where they could pitch their tent for the night. Today, they were just too exhausted to keep going.

“We’re heading down; we’re sick and need to recover,” Vasiliev told Belyankina. “We can barely keep moving.”.
