Colorado Hiker Creates Ultimate Thru-Hike Across His Home State

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that donovan Rice got into thru-hiking almost by accident.
  • Industry observers note that “I thought, there’s no way somebody can walk from Mexico to Canada.
  • From there, it was a slippery slope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that donovan Rice got into thru-hiking almost by accident. Already outdoorsy, he graduated from long hikes to planning to climb all 53 of Colorado’s 14,000’ers (mountains above 14,000 feet, or 4,267m). While researching which peaks required overnight camping, he realized that some people’s hikes just keep going.

Industry observers note that “I thought, there’s no way somebody can walk from Mexico to Canada. That’s just ridiculous,” Rice explained. “I fell in love with that idea.”.

From there, it was a slippery slope. First came the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), from the Mexican border in California to the Canadian border in British Columbia. Then he did the Continental Divide Trail (CDT), tracing the Rocky Mountains from Latest Mexico to the Montana-Canada border. Before he knew it, he had a trail name — Iceman —and was working the gig economy to free up time for wilderness adventures.

But that’s where most people’s slippery slope levels out. Hiking the 4,988km CDT is as meaty a project as most of us can imagine. But for Rice, it only opened the floodgates. He was fascinated by everything that didn’t make it into famous routes, especially the ridges and mountains he passed in his home state of Colorado that were just off trail.

It has been revealed that “There’s all this stuff the CDT doesn’t hit because it is following the Continental Divide,” he told ExplorersWeb. “So when I got to the end of the Colorado section, about 700 miles, I was thinking, man, if there were a 2,000-mile version of that, it would be my dream thru-hike. Just that non-stop, relentless brutality that is Colorado.”.

Colorado has 14,000′ peaks but also deserts. Photo: Donovan Rice.

Rice started thinking about a massive thru-hike loop of the state. His idea was to stitch together existing trails and form latest ones where necessary.

“I dropped a load of pins across the areas in Colorado I wanted to visit, then I pulled out a public lands layer of the map to see how I might connect the areas,” he explained. “The three core design philosophies were beauty, breadth, and epicness. I wanted to see beautiful views, I wanted to cover as much of Colorado’s diversity as possible, and I wanted to take the most iconic and epic route possible.”.

Unlike places like the UK, there is no “right to roam” in Colorado, so connecting the route to avoid private land was tricky. Occasionally, he had to link bits of public land and sections of trail in the “least worst way,” with short road walks when private property appeared to halt progress.

As he tacked on mountain peaks and the national parks he wanted to explore, his route swelled to a monstrous 3,000km+. His itinerary now included all 11 of Colorado’s national forests, three of its national parks, 13 14,000’ers and 47 13,000’ers.

Recent findings suggest that “This is not an efficient route,” Rice admits. “You could walk the full perimeter of Colorado and then hike the Colorado Trail [an existing 885km trail from Waterton Canyon near Denver to Durango], and then still have kilometers left over [to complete the loop].”.

Industry observers note that the Great Colorado Route. Photo: Donovan Rice.

In a recent development, the route looked epic on paper, but Rice still needed to prove it could actually be thru-hiked. After months of planning, Rice set off on his Great Colorado Route from Gunnison National Park on May 14, 2026. He traveled ultra-light, carrying just six kilos of gear, with just a quilt instead of a sleeping bag and a tarp rather than a tent.

“I wanted it to be lightweight enough that I could be nimble on the mountains while doing these technical traverses,” said Rice. Traveling light was wise. Rice’s Great Colorado Route is challenging, with plenty of scrambling and sustained time at altitude.

According to recent reports, “The crux might be between Bailey and Rocky Mountain National Park. You go over the Mount Evans Wilderness, two 14,000’ers, hop on the Front Range across several 13,000’ers, and then across the Tenmile Range, and then the absolutely brutal Gore Range.”.

Rice spent 141 days tramping his trail, eventually finishing on October 1 after 3,252km. While he describes the route as “definitely not beginner-friendly” — due to plenty of cross-country terrain, off-trail navigation, and route-finding — it doesn’t require mountaineering skills.

Sources indicate that “For me, the real sweet spot is Class three scrambling,” he notes. “Once you get up to Class four, it starts getting really scary, and I had no tolerance at all for true Class five rock climbing.”.

However, he did pack an ice ax, micro-spikes, snow gaiters, and a lightweight helmet to protect against rockfall. He also made an effort to structure the route to provide relief between the most challenging sections, giving the trail an ebb and flow, and potential hikers time to decompress.

Industry observers note that the Ballard to La Junta traverse. Photo: Donovan Rice.

Overall, his focus on scenic beauty over contrived difficulty helped keep the route somewhat accessible. This is important because Rice hopes that other hikers will give it a go. He is building a website that maps the route, segment by segment, with GPS coordinates to help future hikers find the best places to camp or alternative paths depending on trail conditions. This is a May-through-October trail, but Rice stresses that it is unrealistic to expect perfect conditions for four and a half months.

“This is one of those routes where bailouts will have to happen,” Rice explained. “You’ll have to take a low route or an alternate. I’m hoping to revisit some of the areas in the future and establish some of these alternative routes.”.

He aims to get all 29 segments of the initial route fully mapped on The Great Colorado website by the end of the year. It’s a substantial project, almost as big as the hike itself.

Industry observers note that “I need to see how many people will actually give it a try. People can do segments. I’d love to see more thru-hikers do this, but the big challenge is that I think the majority of thru-hikers will look at this and think ‘that’s above my pay grade’.”.

Industry observers note that the Castles, Colorado. Photo: Donovan Rice.

Once he finishes the website, the level of interest might dictate his next steps. “I don’t know what level of formal recognition I want to try for. Do I want to try to get it codified? Or should it stay unofficial and remain just some cool thing someone did that published information on how to do it yourself.”.

Whether or not his Great Colorado Route ever gains the name recognition of the CDT or PCT, Rice has authored something unique, and in a world full of rehashes and copycats, that makes it special.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This morning, rescuers found the bodies of Japanese climbers Hidesuke Taneishi, 40, and Tetsu Hashimoto, 25, on Gangapurna West.

“Both bodies were found at around 6,300m on the south side of Gangapurna West,” the rescue team told The Tourism Times.

Hidesuke Taneishi (left) and Tetsu Hashimoto (right) with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure.

The climbers were attempting the first ascent of the 7,140m mountain and lost contact on October 15 at approximately 7,050m on their summit push.

A search-and-rescue team has been looking for the pair since October 19. Unfortunately, no one knew where they were on the mountain, or even if they were on the mountain at all. Therefore, the search started at Manang village, with no success.

In a recent development, the team included helicopter pilot Sobit Gauchan, high-altitude photographer and climber Manish Maharjan, and IFMGA mountain guide Pansang Rinzee Sherpa. The helicopter dropped Maharjan and Rinzee at 5,750m, and from there they used a drone to search the upper slopes. They scouted the northeast and southwest sides of the mountain, and finally found the remains of the Japanese climbers’ higher camp. Today, they found the bodies on the south side.

As for the cause of the accident, Rinzee told ExplorersWeb that their observations of the terrain pointed to a snow slab collapse.

Several teams have attempted Gangapurna West, located next to the Annapurna massif in Manang district, since it opened to foreign teams in 2014. However, none have summited. The mountain is also known as Asapurna or Lachenal Peak.

Team leader Hidesuke Taneishi was nominated for a Piolet d’Or last year after his first ascent of 6,652m Pholesobi Peak, also in Nepal, via a direct route up its vertiginous north face with Hiroki Yamamoto.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Board games that make players pay bills, borrow, and invest let kids practice money decisions where a mistake costs only play money. Pick one that fits your player’s age and attention span. Afterward, ask why a move worked or didn’t, and connect a rent payment or loan in the game to your family’s own.

A kid can watch a parent pay with a tap of a card all week and never see a bill, a loan balance, or an investment account.

A board game puts all three in front of them. In PayDay, a month of bills comes due on payday, and in Monopoly, a mortgaged property stops collecting rent. The game shows a player what a choice cost. A question afterward about why they made it gets them to strategy differently in the next game.

Each entry gives the ages its publisher recommends and what the game has players do with money.

Start with the ages on the box, then match the game’s length to how long your player will sit still. A game of Monopoly Deal can be over in 15 minutes, and Acquire runs about 90 minutes. PayDay’s rules let players choose how many months to play and say a three-month game with four players takes about an hour. Rich Dad indicates first-timers might need three to four hours for CASHFLOW.

For a shorter game of Monopoly, the rules in the box say to skip house rules: auction any property the player who lands on it won’t buy, never lend money between players, and put no cash on Free Parking.

It has been revealed that for a preschooler, a pretend store with real coins is the place to start. A younger sibling can join an older one’s game as a teammate who handles the money.

According to recent reports, keep the talk short, and have it right after the game. Ask about one move that cost or made money, and let the player explain it before you add anything.

Picture a 10-year-old who comes up short at the end of a PayDay month. She borrows, then pays 10% of the loan every month after that. If she decides to set aside part of each month’s salary in the next game, she has worked out why a budget looks for bills before they arrive.

Sources indicate that tie the game to your family’s money too. A Monopoly rent payment is the moment to say what your household pays in rent or on its mortgage each month. A PayDay loan is the moment to show the interest rate on a credit card statement.

Set up a rematch within a week or two, so the player can try the change they described.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every year, the Banff Centre Mountain Film and Book Festival celebrates the best mountain and adventure writing, film, and photography. The literary highlight of this alpine-themed celebration is the Banff Mountain Book Competition, with eight categories and one grand prize. The jury will award the grand prize at the festival, but the category winners have been announced.

Sources indicate that first, the two Special Jury Mentions. Jack Plant’s Spirit of the Great Bear showcases his spectacular photography of the Great Bear Forest. Meanwhile, Ian Nicholson’s Glacier Travel & Crevasse Rescue: Essential Skills for Snow Travel does exactly what it notes on the tin. “Of all the skill sets required for mountain climbing, perhaps none are as intimidating as glacier travel. But with carefully crafted instructions and illustrations, Nicholson takes us behind the curtain,” jury member Lauren DeLaunay Miller explains.

It has been revealed that the Mountain Literature award went to Lone Wolf: Walking the Line Between Civilization and Wildness by Adam Weymouth. Weymouth dives into the place of wild animals in modern Europe, a continent “undergoing profound climatic, environmental, and political changes.”.

It has been revealed that black Bear: A Story of Siblinghood and Survival by Trina Moyles won the Environmental Literature category. “Black Bear seamlessly weaves together two complex storylines, laying bare Moyles’ relationships with her brother and with the wildlife she meets while working in a fire watch tower in Alberta.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Mountain Article prize, awarded to a magazine piece rather than a book, went to The Misfits by Chad Heddleston. Heddleston chose to profile rock climbing couple Jan and Herb Conn. “These two exist in the spirit and austerity of the pioneering European climbers of the early 20th century. The writing highlights their uniqueness and the integrity of their life choices,” jury member David Chambre said.

According to recent reports, pioneering rock climbers Jan and Herb Conn. Photo: Dwight Deal.

The Adventure Travel prize went to North to the Future: An Offline Adventure through the Changing Wilds of Alaska by Ben Weissenbach. “Weissenbach — an L.A. native with little prior wilderness experience — treks through the Alaskan tundra with a series of eccentric environmental scientists and returns with a fresh perspective on technology and a revitalized sense of wonder for the natural world.”.

Cabin Wild: Alpine Bivouac Huts by Ben Tibbetts won the Guidebook award. “A captivating volume that invites us to see the Alps in a upcoming light, through an intimate journey around a selection of bivouac huts across Italy, Switzerland, and France,” according to jury member Rob Lovell.

According to recent reports, the Mountain Image award went to Fjell: A Faithful Witness by Orsolya Haarberg. “A highly original book that takes us on a journey through the Norwegian highlands. It is as much an art book as a book about mountains,” explains jury member David Chambre.

Finally, The Great Mixed Climbs of Scotland by Guy Robertson & Hamish Frost won the Climbing Literature prize. “The Great Mixed Climbs of Scotland combines stunning photography and evocative essays in a truly spectacular ode to Scottish winter climbing. By profiling vital routes through the eyes of the climbers who created them, Guy Robertson and Hamish Frost have created an exceptional book.”.

The category-winning authors get cash prizes and a chance to win the grand prize at the festival on November 5.

Industry News: Pitch Angel Investors Who Know Your Industry – and Know What a SAFE Costs You

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that start with angel investors from your own industry, who bring advice and contacts along with the money.
  • They funded 22.6% of the deals brought to them in 2024, the University of Upcoming Hampshire’s Center for Venture Research found.
  • According to recent reports, most angel groups invest in markets where some of their members have expertise, the Angel Capital Association says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that start with angel investors from your own industry, who bring advice and contacts along with the money. Reach them through local angel groups and introductions from founders they’ve backed. Before you take a check, work out what share of your manufacturer the deal sells.

Angels turn most founders down. They funded 22.6% of the deals brought to them in 2024, the University of Upcoming Hampshire’s Center for Venture Research found.

According to recent reports, most angel groups invest in markets where some of their members have expertise, the Angel Capital Association says. An angel who has worked in your field can judge your plan quickly and introduce you to customers and later investors.

Search the association’s member directory, which lists angel groups by state and area of focus, and apply to the ones in your industry the way each group’s website asks. Ask founders in your field to introduce you to the angels who backed them, including any who lead a syndicate, which pools backers’ money into one check.

In a recent development, bring a short pitch and a one-page summary that show a large market and early traction, such as paying customers, and know your numbers cold. Take money only from accredited investors, who meet the SEC’s income, net-worth, or professional tests, since raising from anyone else brings extra disclosure rules.

Expect a SAFE, short for simple agreement for future equity, or less often a convertible note, a loan. Either usually turns into shares at your first priced round, the first time you sell shares at a set price. SAFEs made up 93% of the earliest-stage rounds on Carta, which tracks startup ownership, in the second quarter of 2026. On the standard SAFE, the angels’ share is at least their investment divided by the valuation cap, the highest firm value the SAFE converts at. Six angels who put $250,000 into standard SAFEs with an $8 million cap would own at least 3.1% ($250,000 divided by $8 million) just before your priced round problems new shares.

Most SAFEs convert right at their cap. Only 29% of priced seed rounds raised in 2026’s first nine months by startups with SAFEs converted those SAFEs below the cap, Carta’s latest report shows. Keep a running total of the share every SAFE takes, and have a startup lawyer read each one before you sign.

#91007. The Mountain That Looked Impossible: Muztagh Tower, 1956

📅 23 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1672 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Mountain That Looked Impossible: Muztagh Tower, 1956

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For nearly half a century, a single photograph defined one of the Karakoram’s most striking peaks.
  • Recent findings suggest that in the summer of 1956, two independent expeditions arrived on opposite sides of the peak, each convinced they were looking at one of the range’s last great unclimbed problems.
  • Vittorio Sella was born in 1859 in Biella, Italy, into a family connected to the mountains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For nearly half a century, a single photograph defined one of the Karakoram’s most striking peaks. Taken in 1909 and reproduced in books and journals, it demonstrated Muztagh Tower as a vertical blade, a slender tooth of rock and ice rising from the glaciers with no obvious weakness. Generations of climbers studied it and concluded that the mountain was impossible to summit.

Recent findings suggest that in the summer of 1956, two independent expeditions arrived on opposite sides of the peak, each convinced they were looking at one of the range’s last great unclimbed problems. But the photograph had misled them.

Vittorio Sella was born in 1859 in Biella, Italy, into a family connected to the mountains. His uncle, Quintino Sella, had helped found the Club Alpino Italiano, and his father, Giuseppe Venanzio Sella, was a pioneer of early photography who published the first crucial Italian treatise on the subject.

It has been revealed that vittorio Sella combined serious alpinism with large-format photography. He made the first winter ascent of the Matterhorn in 1882, followed by the first winter traverse of Mont Blanc. Throughout his career, he carried heavy glass-plate cameras into the high Alps, the Caucasus, Alaska, the Ruwenzori, and the Karakoram.

According to recent reports, sella’s photographic technique was excellent. His plates were large, the detail exceptional, and the compositions carefully chosen. His work was much admired, including by American photographer Ansel Adams. In a 1946 article for the Sierra Club Bulletin, Adams paid tribute to Sella’s work, writing:.

Recent findings suggest that “The purity of Sella’s interpretations move the spectator to a religious awe. Sella has brought to us not only the facts and forms of far-off splendours of the world, but the essence of experience which finds a spiritual response in the inner recesses of our mind and heart.”.

Vittorio Sella. Photo: Alpine Club Photo Library.

Sella’s most crucial Himalayan photographs came from the 1909 K2 expedition led by Luigi Amedeo, Duke of the Abruzzi.

Filippo De Filippi’s official account of the expedition, Karakoram and Western Himalaya 1909 (published in English in 1912), was illustrated throughout with Sella’s images. Those photographs remain among the finest early records of the range. One of them, a telephoto view of Muztagh Tower, became famous far beyond the expedition report, and inadvertently sparked a legendary mountaineering myth.

It has been revealed that muztagh Tower (7,276m) is located in the Baltoro Muztagh of the Karakoram, on the border between Pakistan’s Gilgit-Baltistan and China’s Xinjiang. It rises between the Baltoro and Sarpo Laggo Glaciers, just north of the main Baltoro corridor leading toward K2.

The peak has two summits only a short distance apart. The eastern peak is the true summit, and the western summit is a few metres lower. From most angles, the mountain is a substantial massif with steep but not uniformly vertical faces. From one particular viewpoint it collapses into something that looks far more extreme.

Muztagh Tower taken from the Upper Baltoro Glacier in 1919 by Vittorio Sella. The tower appears as an impregnable tooth. The photo inspired mountaineers for decades. Photo: Vittorio Sella.

Industry observers note that sella took the image of Muztagh Tower from the upper Baltoro Glacier, looking northwest toward the mountain. The twin summits lined up almost perfectly. The long telephoto lens compressed the intervening ground and presented the peak as a narrow, knife-edged tower whose walls appeared to fall nearly vertically from summit to glacier.

From other angles the peak revealed broader ridges and less precipitous slopes, but this single compressed view was the one that circulated widely. The effect was really dramatic, but as later climbers discovered, also misleading. In 1941, Sella’s photo of Muztagh Tower appeared in a mountaineering book under the caption “The Last Citadel.” The image fixed the mountain’s reputation for decades.

Industry observers note that muztagh Tower, 1909. Photo: Vittorio Sella.

In 1956, a British team and a French team both set out for Muztagh Tower, drawn in large part by Sella’s photograph.

Sources indicate that the British team, led by John Hartog and consisting of Joe Brown, Ian McNaught-Davis, Tom Patey, and liaison officer Captain Riaz Mohammad, chose the Northwest Ridge. They planned to approach via the Muztagh and Chagaran glaciers on the western side of the peak.

It has been revealed that the French party, led by Guido Magnone, included Andre Contamine, Paul Keller, Robert Paragot, Francois Florence, and liaison officer Ali Usman. They worked from the eastern side, aiming for what became the eastern arête after reconnaissance ruled out the North Ridge. The two groups operated independently on opposite flanks of the mountain.

The British established Base Camp on the Muztagh Glacier on May 28, 1956, at 4,282m. Through the first half of June, they placed camps on the Chagaran Glacier, avoiding the worst of the lower icefall by climbing the northern moraine and then threading seracs. Camp 3 was set on the west col at 6,355m after a steep ice wall. They reached the col on June 16, but took until the end of the month to move tents, fuel, and food up.

From there the route followed the exposed crest of the West Ridge, a mixed line of rock, snow and ice that required fixed ropes on the steeper sections. Brown made a key traverse around a rock cliff on the South Face. Camp 4 was placed on the ridge itself at 6,439m.

Above the high camp, the climbing continued up a narrow couloir and then mixed ground. The final technical obstacle was a short rock leaf between the two summits, graded alpine V and exposed on both sides.

According to recent reports, on July 6, Brown and McNaught-Davis reached the western summit. The following day, Hartog and Patey, after supporting the first pair, crossed the connecting ridge and stood on the slightly higher eastern summit. Both pairs had to bivouac on the descent. Hartog suffered frostbitten toes. All four climbers reached the top.

Muztagh Tower. Photo: Hunza Adventure Tours.

Recent findings suggest that the French established their Base Camp at 4,496m on June 12 after approaching from the Younghusband Glacier. Their reconnaissance quickly indicated the North Ridge was impossible, so they moved onto the eastern branch of the glacier.

According to recent reports, they fixed ropes through an icefall and up a rock-and-ice spur, placing successive camps until Camp 4 stood at the foot of the summit pyramid at 6,300m. On July 6, as bad weather closed in, they spotted the British climbers moving on the upper heights.

After the two-day storm cleared, the French regained the ridge, overcame two substantial rock towers, and bivouacked high on the mountain. On July 12, Magnone, Paragot, Contamine, and Keller reached the main summit through deep snow, six days after the British first topped out. After summiting, they descended to Camp 4 after dark. Dr. Florence had waited at high camp for more than 40 hours without radio contact during the summit push.

In a recent development, the British party therefore made the first ascent of Muztagh Tower. The French completed an independent second ascent six days later. Both teams discovered that the mountain, while technically demanding and exposed, offered viable lines. The route, while serious, proved less relentlessly steep than Sella’s photograph had suggested.

It has been revealed that the two expeditions were not engaged in a formal competition. They approached from opposite sides, followed separate routes, and maintained cordial relations. The British simply reached the summit first. The French, seeing the British already on top, continued their own line to completion.

Far from a bitter nationalistic race, the two teams demonstrated alpine solidarity. The French team chose the east side specifically to avoid interfering with British progress on the western side. Rather than abandoning their push in defeat after spotting the British on the summit, the French celebrated their colleagues’ historic achievement and resolutely pushed forward to fulfill their own objective. When Hartog suffered severe frostbite during his descent, the French team stepped in to provide vital assistance and support during the evacuation.

According to recent reports, the southeast side of Muztagh Tower, showing the route. Photo: Guido Magnone for The Himalayan Journal.

In a recent development, since 1956, Muztagh Tower has remained one of the least visited major peaks in the Karakoram. A British team in 1984 repeated the Northwest Ridge (Mal Duff, Tony Brindle, Jon Tinker, and Sandy Allan), though they reached the slightly lower west summit rather than the true east summit. In 1990, a Swedish party consisting of Göran Kropp and Rafael Jensen also successfully scaled the Northwest Ridge.

It has been revealed that in August 2008, Slovenian alpinists Pavle Kozjek and Dejan Miskovic made a groundbreaking alpine-style push up the steep Northeast Face. They successfully reached the upper ridge crest, but ferocious winds ended their push. Tragically, just after beginning their descent, a ridge cornice collapsed, and Kozjek fell to his death.

The 2,000m Northeast Spur of Muztagh Tower showing the line “Think Twice.” Photo: American Alpine Journal.

According to recent reports, four years later, Russians Sergey Nilov, Dmitry Golovchenko, and Alexander Lange made the historic first ascent of the massive Northeast Spur. Their grueling 17-day climb via a newly introduced route named “Think Twice” reached the true summit, earning them the prestigious Piolets d’Or. The Russian team indicated in their expedition report that Muztagh Tower was 7,284m.

The 1956 French route has never been fully repeated to the main peak, and no further ascents of the true summit have been confirmed since the 2012 Russian expedition. Still, climbers continue to push limits here, most notably in 2019, with the first ascent of the Black Tooth (6,718m), a difficult lower spire on the mountain’s ridge.

Sources indicate that muztagh Tower (top left) and its Southeast Ridge, with a high point on the Black Tooth (6,719m). The solid line, with the two marked bivouac sites, is the line of ascent to Black Tooth followed by Simon Messner and Martin Sieberer in 2019. Photo: Simon Messner/American Alpine Journal.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, with an entire river to descend, the film wastes no time getting right into it.
  • Forty years ago, there was a road up to Lake Mayuin, the volcanic pool from with Rio Cuervo flows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This full-length adventure documentary follows kayaker Dane Jackson and a small team down Chile’s remote and wild Rio Cuervo.

In a recent development, with an entire river to descend, the film wastes no time getting right into it. Dane Jackson rolls out into the complicated business of trip logistics, trying to find a way to get the team and their equipment to the beginning of the river. Besides him, the team consists of the trip’s mastermind, Kilian Astorga, and kayakers Tom Dolle, Eirik Hansen, Adrian Mattern, and David Sodomka.

Forty years ago, there was a road up to Lake Mayuin, the volcanic pool from with Rio Cuervo flows. It’s gone now, so they turn to helicopter transport. With their gear dangling below on a rope, the chopper carries them up into the mountain, depositing kayaks and kayakers alike on the lakeshore. They set up camp and settle in to begin the first descent of the Rio Cuervo.

It has been revealed that the team scouts the head of the river, swelled with recent rainfall. Photo: Screenshot.

The dense forest and sometimes steep banks add another layer of difficulty as they begin to make their way downstream. They have to plan ahead, as there are stretches where it is impossible to bail if the rapids become too much. This means more portaging, which is painfully slow due to the thick vegetation.

When they do hit the rapids, on-board cameras capture the frenetic energy of whitewater kayaking. But the film makes no attempt to conceal the reality of a first descent. Much of their time is spent scouting ahead by drone, poring over satellite images, portaging, and standing about debating logistics.

It has been revealed that sunset arrives before the end of their portage. Camping in the jungle makes for an uncomfortable night. Photo: Screenshot.

Jackson and the rest of the crew soldier on, though, cracking nerdy jokes (the jungle is compared to both Dagobah and Fangorn Forest) and making the best of bad weather and rough camping. In the final few days, conditions improve, and they can spend more time on the water.

The contrast between their slow, grueling push forward and the wild speed on the river brings refreshing energy to the kayaking sections. When the river finally widens as they glide into the sea, it feels like a hard-won victory.

In a recent development, running a 3.5km gorge. Photo: Screenshot.

Early in the production of a certain musical, Broadway director Harold Prince attempted to ask Andrew Lloyd Weber what the deeper political allegory or social commentary was behind the composer’s feline opus. Weber famously took a long pause and replied: “Hal, this is just about cats.”.

In a recent development, this movie is about kayaking. Many outdoor adventure films use the genre, and the adventure story, to explore grand themes, and some do so successfully. But when they fall flat, is it more annoying than I can begin to express. For that reason, I deeply respect the clarity of purpose evinced by Dan Jackson and First Descent Rio Cuervo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tutoring pays by the hour, and the rate depends on what you teach, so price each subject and grade level you offer by what tutors near you charge for it. Find your first students through parents, teachers, and school counselors, and use tutoring sites, which keep a cut, to fill the hours referrals don’t.

Private tutoring takes no teaching license, just a subject you know well, and you set your own hours, so it fits around a day job or classes.

What you can charge depends on what you teach. Wiingy, a tutoring site, tracked nearly 14,000 tutor listings for its 2026 price index and found SAT math averaging about $60 an hour, against about $45 for Spanish. Rates for the same subject also vary widely from city to city. Charge one rate for everything, and you either undercharge for test prep or price yourself out of everyday homework help.

Sources indicate that list each subject and level you could teach, such as SAT math, middle school algebra, and early reading. Search a tutoring site like Wyzant for each one the way a parent near you would. Its results show every tutor’s hourly rate, and the middle of those rates is a fair starting point for yours.

Industry observers note that find your first students locally: tell parents you know, ask teachers and school counselors to pass your name along, and post in your town’s parent groups. Wyzant also brings students, but it keeps 25% of your posted rate on the ones it finds you. A retired engineer who charges $60 an hour for SAT math and fills six hours a week through two parents’ referrals is paid the full $360 a week. The same six hours booked through Wyzant would pay him $270, so save tutoring sites for the hours referrals leave open.

Run it as a small business. Put your cancellation and payment terms in writing, such as 24 hours’ notice to cancel, and keep a background check ready for families who ask. Deposit tutoring income in a separate bank account and set part of each payment aside for taxes. Once your self-employment profit reaches $400 in a year, the IRS charges self-employment tax of 15.3% for Social Security and Medicare, on top of income tax.

A full schedule is the signal to raise the rate you quote fresh families, while families you already work with keep the rate they started with.

  • Most of the route, roughly 70%, is unpaved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that colorado couple Jules Stennes and Patch Doyle have cycled 6,124km along the newly opened Golden Gravel Trail. The Adventure Cycling Association created the route this year to celebrate its 50th anniversary.

The trail crosses eight states — Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Idaho, and Oregon — and stretches from Cape Girardeau on the banks of the Mississippi River to the small town of Port Orford on the edge of the Pacific Ocean.

Most of the route, roughly 70%, is unpaved. It is the organization’s longest off-road cycling trail, 1,120km longer than the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route.

The Golden Gravel Trail route. Photo: The Adventure Cycling Association.

Stennes and Doyle finished in Cape Girardeau after 73 days, averaging an impressive 80km and around 12 hours of pedaling per day. “About 90% of it is mental,” they told Heartland News. “You might be tired, but you just keep on moving.”.

The couple are both experienced long-distance cyclists who have previously finished Montana’s Big Sky Spectaculaire in six days and nine hours in 2022 (a self-supported 1,400km ultra-endurance race), among other bikepacking trips.

According to recent reports, jules Stennes and Patch Doyle during the 2022 Big Sky Spectaculaire. Photo: Bikepacking.com.

Likewise, the Adventure Cycling Association suggests riders should be self-supported for the Golden Gravel Trail. Riders are advised to carry two or three days’ worth of food for the route’s most isolated sections, and up to a day’s worth of water. This is particularly important in the more arid sections, such as eastern Oregon. In Colorado, Utah, and Idaho, the trail traverses subranges of the Rockies and crosses the route’s highest point, Cumberland Pass at 3,668 m, in Colorado.

Stennes and Doyle say their journey included thunderstorms, aggressive farm dogs, and “countless hills.”.

Search teams have found the body of Wolfgang Waschiczek, 57, of Germany, who went missing after he reached Camp 3 on his way down from the summit. Evidence highlights he fell 1,700m to his death.

In a recent development, waschiczek was one among over 200 climbers who lined up toward the summit of Ama Dablam this past weekend. He reached the top on October 25 with guide Sonam Sherpa, but for some reason the two of them stopped descending at a rather high point on the mountain.

“The pair decided to stay at Camp 3 overnight after borrowing a sleeping bag and other gear from other climbers,” his expedition outfitter, Real Himalaya Nepal, told The Tourism Times.

In a recent development, climbers above Camp 3 on Ama Dablam. Photo: Dorjee Gyalzen Sherpa.

Recent findings suggest that according to the outfitter, the climbers prepared to continue down this morning. Lama asked his client to stay in place while he returned the sleeping bag to the tent where he had borrowed it. When the Sherpa returned, Waschiczek was nowhere to be found, but his crampons were still there, which suggested a freak fall. A search helicopter was called, and the remains of the climber were found this afternoon at around 4,500m.

Waschiczek is the first fatality on Ama Dablam this season.

Industry observers note that together with Manaslu, Ama Dablam is the most popular fall mountain in Nepal. The latest revision from Nepal’s Department of Tourism on October 17 demonstrated that over 300 foreign climbers had applied for a climbing permit. That day, the rope-fixing team opened the route to the top, and a massive summit wave started a couple of days later.

In a recent development, virtually all foreign climbers are guided by one or two Sherpas, so the summit rates and numbers are remarkable. Local media estimate that over 200 climbers, among locals and foreigners, have topped out so far this season. Further teams should join them over the rest of October and November. However, no matter how tamed with ropes and anchors Ama Dablam gets, a fall from its steep slopes is usually lethal.

The upper part of Ama Dablam at sunset. Photo: 8K Expeditions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In many states, public colleges waive tuition for residents once they reach 60, 62, or 65, so you can take regular college classes for little more than books and fees. Ask a nearby public college’s registrar for its tuition waiver for older students, and find out when waiver students may register.

The other rules vary by state. Florida law lets the state’s public universities and colleges waive tuition and fees for residents 60 and older who audit classes, meaning they sit in without earning credit. At the University of North Georgia, Georgia residents 62 and older can take classes for credit or audit them, but they can’t register for fall or spring terms until the first day of classes. Kentucky law requires the state’s public colleges to waive all tuition and fees for residents 65 and older unless classes are full.

Under North Georgia’s waiver, a 66-year-old Georgia resident taking two history classes a semester pays for her books, supplies, and any lab fees, but no tuition.

According to recent reports, to find your state’s version, call the registrar or continuing education office at a nearby public college and ask for its tuition waiver for older students. Bring proof of age and residency, such as a driver’s license, and ask whether you can earn credit and which fees you still owe. Where no nearby school offers one, ask your state’s higher education agency which campuses do.

Sources indicate that if no seat opens, look up the nearest Osher Lifelong Learning Institute. The institutes, at colleges in all 50 states, run noncredit classes for people 50 and older, with no tests or grades, for fees that vary by institute. A community college’s continuing education classes and universities’ free online courses are other options.

For a waiver seat, call the registrar a semester ahead, since you may need to apply for admission by the college’s usual deadline before the waiver covers a class.

  • It has been revealed that manaslu Base Camp tents buried under the snow after the September storm in Nepal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for the second time in just over a month, a violent storm is approaching Nepal and threatening two meters of fresh snow on already overloaded mountains. This upcoming setback comes at the height of the trekking season and also affects several climbing teams, including those engaged in alpine-style expeditions in remote areas.

The first storm hit Nepal toward the end of September and abruptly ended the climbing season on Manaslu. Worst of all, it caused an avalanche that killed 16 Base Camp staff on Himlung. The mountain remained open to commercial expeditions despite the accident, and several guided teams are currently launching their summit pushes.

It has been revealed that manaslu Base Camp tents buried under the snow after the September storm in Nepal. Photo: Shiddi Ghising.

A low-pressure front that formed in the Bay of Bengal has now developed into a deep depression and will turn into a full cyclone tomorrow. It is expected to hit Nepal on Wednesday or Thursday through the end of the week.

The Nepal National Mountain Guides Association, in association with Senior Meteorologist Krishna Bhakta Manandhar, has put out a detailed forecast. They note that clouds spreading out from this system will hit Nepal’s mountains on October 28, especially above 6,500-7,000m in the eastern part of Nepal, including the Khumbu and Kanchenjunga regions. This will spread over the next two days, causing heavy rains throughout Nepal and snow at higher altitudes.

Industry observers note that authorities and local media have urged trekkers and climbers to modify their looks and avoid river areas and high passes. The main concern is for those presently in remote areas without InReach, Starlink, or satphones.

Sources indicate that trekkers should check with local agencies, especially those heading for the Annapurna and Manaslu regions. Several passes there were already cut or in poor condition after the previous storm and subsequent floods.

A Russian team in the Kangchenjunga region is acclimatizing to climb 7,710m Jannu. According to their latest report, they plan to touch 7,000m before attempting their main goal.

According to recent reports, fellow Russians attempting the West Ridge of Everest have retreated to Kathmandu to rest and recover, so they should not be affected. Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov, all climbing without supplemental oxygen, are enduring some lung problems. They returned to Base Camp from their second foray up the mountain last Friday, without reaching 7,500m, as they’d hoped.

After climbing in the Cholu range, Jost Kobusch of Germany and his small team moved to the Manaslu area for the second stage of his acclimatization before attempting Everest solo in winter, also without oxygen and via the West Ridge. However, the poor state of the trails after the recent floods and the approaching cyclone have thwarted his intends.

“The flood cut our planned path and, according to forecasts, the incoming cyclone will leave up to two meters of snow,” Kobusch told ExplorersWeb from Samagaon, where the team is pondering their options.

In a recent development, to make money teaching English online, apply where your background fits. Without a teaching certificate, start on a conversation app, which pays a flat rate. With one, use a lesson marketplace, where you set your own price and the certificate justifies charging more. Then make yourself available when students book most.

Neither kind requires a degree or a teaching certificate. Credentials change how much you can earn.

In a recent development, without a certificate, start with Cambly, a conversation app that pays $0.17 for each minute you’re in a lesson, or $10.20 for a full hour. An hour with gaps between calls pays less than $10.20, and Cambly is temporarily limiting how many upcoming tutors it takes.

In a recent development, with a certificate, set your own price on Preply, a lesson marketplace where English tutors charge $15 to $25 an hour on average. Preply keeps the whole fee for each new student’s trial lesson and, while you’re new, 33% of every lesson after that, a cut that falls to 18% as your teaching hours add up. At $15 an hour, you’d keep $10.05, a bit less than Cambly’s $10.20 for the same hour. A TEFL (Teaching English as a Foreign Language) certificate can let you charge more, Preply’s own guide to becoming a tutor says, and at $25 you’d keep $16.75 after the same cut.

Count the costs, too. You need a quiet room, a headset with a microphone, and a reliable internet connection. Both platforms treat you as an independent contractor, so once your net earnings reach $400 in a year, you owe the IRS a 15.3% self-employment tax for Social Security and Medicare, on top of income tax. Set aside part of every payout for both in a separate savings account.

Set your hours around demand, not just your free time. Preply’s calendar shades the times students in your subject are most likely to book, and Cambly’s Priority Hours send you calls from new students during hours you claim. A parent who teaches from 6 to 8 a.m. Eastern can finish before the kids wake up, while it’s evening for learners in Japan and South Korea.

Keep those hours the same every week. Cambly claims a consistent schedule helps attract regular students, and Preply says students are more likely to stay with a tutor who’s always free at the same time.

Breaking: Mont Blanc Has Grown Almost Two Meters — But Not in the Way You Think

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, these days, topographic surveys typically show that a mountain’s altitude is decreasing due to shrinking snowcaps.
  • In a recent development, mont Blanc is now 1.88 meters taller than it was three years ago, according to a recent report by France’s IGN (National Geographic Institute).
  • It has been revealed that however, it may be wise to wait before changing the figure in climbing guides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, these days, topographic surveys typically show that a mountain’s altitude is decreasing due to shrinking snowcaps. But strangely, Mont Blanc, the highest peak in the Alps, has grown significantly since its latest measurement in 2023.

In a recent development, mont Blanc is now 1.88 meters taller than it was three years ago, according to a recent report by France’s IGN (National Geographic Institute). The new official altitude is now 4,807.47 meters (15,772.5 feet) above sea level.

It has been revealed that however, it may be wise to wait before changing the figure in climbing guides. Measurements are carried out every two years, and each time the registered altitude varies:.

Graphic showing the results of the last few measurements on Mont Blanc, by LaChangingMeteo.

In a recent development, mont Blanc’s “summit is constantly shifting,” Jean des Garets, chief geometer in the Haute-Savoie department, told Le Monde. “Each individual measurement is not significant in itself.”.

So, what’s with the yearly differences? Obviously, it’s the variation in the thick but ever-changing snowcap that covers the summit.

According to recent reports, the mountain’s rocky summit measures around 4,792m above sea level. The snow cover varies with the seasons. The difference from the previous measurement shows that 2023 was much drier at summit altitude.

The survey team on itsir way to the summit of Mont Blanc.. Photo: ING.

A team from the Order of Chartered Surveyors (Ordre des géomètres-experts) acclimatized first by climbing Bishorn (4,153m). They then spent some days measuring several points around the mountain. Finally, they climbed Mont Blanc via the normal route on September 15-16.

Once on top, they pinpointed the highest point using a GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) pole, which measures altitude in real time.

The recent survey featured an interesting novelty. In addition to altitude, the survey also measured Mont Blanc’s gravity by installing a gravimeter on the summit for the first time ever. This measured the force with which the Earth attracts the device. In so doing, they wanted to determine whether the summit has sunk, regardless of ice cover.

The gravimeter on the summit of Mont Blanc, September 16. Photo: ING France.

“When the height of Mont Blanc changes, we can’t know for sure whether the ground or the rock has moved or if the ice has melted,” explains Olivier Jamet.

Gravity provides the missing information: mass. If the ice has melted, there is less material under the instrument, but the rock has moved closer to it. Distinguishing these two effects requires a model of the ice cap and the massif, and above all, repeated measurements at the same location. And the effort is worthwhile, especially now that the effects of climate change on Alpine glaciers are becoming increasingly apparent.

The gravimeter on the top of Mont Blanc measured the gravity at 9.7944689 m/s².

“For comparison, this value is 9.81 m/s² in Marseille (located at sea level) and 9.8043046 m/s² in Saint-Gervais-Le Fayet (580m above sea level),” ING reports. “This difference in value, even if it seems small, allows for the detection of changes in mass, particularly in the mass of the ice. Repeated over time, these gravity measurements will thus contribute to improving the determination of the altitude of the highest peak in Western Europe.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that start as a virtual assistant by selling one service you’ve done in a past job, such as managing an inbox and calendar or keeping the books, instead of offering help with anything.
  • Recent findings suggest that business owners hire a virtual assistant to hand off a specific task.
  • It has been revealed that your past jobs tell you which service to sell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that start as a virtual assistant by selling one service you’ve done in a past job, such as managing an inbox and calendar or keeping the books, instead of offering help with anything. Price it by the hour or as a flat monthly package, and pitch it first to people who already know your work.

Recent findings suggest that business owners hire a virtual assistant to hand off a specific task. An offer that names the task and its price is easy to accept, while “I can help with anything” leaves the owner to work out both.

It has been revealed that your past jobs tell you which service to sell. A former executive assistant can manage an owner’s inbox and calendar, an office manager can keep a small company’s books, and someone from a call center can answer customer emails and chats.

Base your price on what employers pay for the same work. In May 2025, the Bureau of Labor Statistics put the median employee wage at $21.53 an hour for customer service representatives, $23.23 for secretaries and administrative assistants, and $24.36 for bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks. Set your rate above the figure for your kind of work. As a contractor, you pay self-employment tax, both the employer’s and the employee’s share of Social Security and Medicare, and nobody pays you for sick days or hours spent finding clients.

Industry observers note that charge by the hour for work that comes and goes. For weekly tasks, sell a flat monthly package that spells out what it covers. Say a former office manager keeps the books for three local contractors, about two hours a week each, for a flat $350 a month per client. That’s about $40 an hour and $1,050 a month.

It has been revealed that pitch former bosses, coworkers, and clients first, since they’ve seen your work. Then look for clients through local business groups, like your chamber of commerce, and freelance marketplaces. Put each client on a short contract that lists the tasks, the rate, when you’re paid, and how either side can end it.

The Federal Trade Commission warns about fake virtual assistant jobs that pay with a check. The fake employer asks you to deposit it, keep part as your pay, and forward the rest to another person. Then the check bounces, and your bank wants the full amount back. A real client never asks you to forward part of a payment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In April, Robert Cowden, 52, set off on foot from Newly introduced Haven, Kansas, on a two-stage journey across the United States. First, he planned to walk nearly 2,000km to Pittsburgh, then canoe 3,200km downriver to the Gulf of Mexico. With him is his dog, Enzo, a pointer-mix.

It has been revealed that robert Cowden and Enzo. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition.

When he left New Haven with Enzo, Cowden was at a low point. His battle with alcohol addiction had cost him his job, car, and home. Entering a residential treatment program would leave Enzo with no place to go. Now sober and with housing waiting for him after the end of his journey, Cowden sees his expedition as part of the larger effort to rebuild his life.

Sources indicate that during the walking stage, Cowden towed his camping gear and supplies in a cart, which Enzo could ride in to take a break from walking. Setting out with very little, Cowden has relied on the kindness of strangers, both online and on the trail, to continue his expedition.

“The number one warning you’re going to get on a walk across America is, ‘Be careful, there’s creepy people and bad people,'” Cowden recalled, speaking to a local KOMU 8 reporter while passing through Missouri. Instead, he’s been overwhelmingly met with generosity and helpfulness.

Cowden demonstrates the wear on his trail shoes, as Enzo looks on. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition.

According to recent reports, cowden completed the walking stage in September. Now, he’s on the Ohio River and hopes to reach the Gulf by the end of 2026. While the second stage lets him and Enzo get off their feet, it has its own challenges. They released the canoe into the Allegheny River at Pittsburgh. It soon joined the Ohio, and lengthy stretches of slow water pushed Cowden to paddle continuously.

Sources indicate that it’s 1,579km down the Ohio to its confluence with the Mississippi in Illinois, which Cowden and Enzo aim to complete in under 40 days. They’re at the moment on pace, averaging about 20km a day.

Cowden posts regular updates on Facebook and on the expedition’s webpage.

#90992. Industry News: The Hidden Benefit Of Being Retired In A Bear Market

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1984 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Hidden Benefit Of Being Retired In A Bear Market

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s.
  • According to recent reports, as every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival.
  • We're not in an official bear market, yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s. Then halfway through the application, I wiped away my tears and took a deep breath.

According to recent reports, as every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival. If you can make it through the downturn, good things usually await on the other side.

We're not in an official bear market, yet. But plenty of individual tech names have already fallen by over 20%, and when you're overweight those names, the index's official status doesn't matter much.

So I thought it might be helpful for those who are retired, or who are close, to discuss the positives of going through a downturn. We'll also review how long downturns usually last so we can better prepare.

As the midterm elections indicated, a lot of people are not happy with the way our country has been led. But the discontent didn't appear overnight. The stock market was simply acting as a giant dose of Lidocaine.

In a recent development, as long as stocks kept going up, we could more easily bear higher oil prices, higher food prices, higher housing costs, higher college tuition costs, and explosive medical costs. After all, our investment returns were growing faster than inflation. $6 for a gallon of gas stings a lot less when your brokerage account is up $50,000 for the year.

But that tolerance for rising costs disappears the moment our investments start losing money. Suddenly, $89 a pound for wagyu feels personal.

When the wealth effect vanishes, consumers cut back. Fewer dinners out. Fewer vacations. The newly introduced car gets pushed out another year. With declining corporate profitability, companies accelerate layoffs to protect margins. The newly unemployed tighten spending even further.

Rinse and repeat until economists officially declare a recession six months after everybody already felt it.

It has been revealed that if you see the writing on the wall, you want want to get ahead of the layoffs by negotiating your own severance package. If you do, you will probably have an easier time getting a much better exit offer than being lumped with the masses.

In a recent development, if you're newly retired, your biggest fear is sequence of returns risk. That's the risk of suffering big losses early in retirement while you're also withdrawing money to live on. Do that for too long and your portfolio may never recover.

It has been revealed that lose enough and you get forced back to work. Nobody who has tasted freedom wants to return to Monday morning status meetings and performance reviews from someone half their age.

It has been revealed that retirees who live off their investments should feel worse about a bear market more than the average worker. We don’t have a paycheck to cushion the blow. We may not have much spare cash flow to buy the dip either.

But here's the key point. If your investments can survive the correction or bear market, you should actually feel good during a downturn. Not ecstatic, but relatively good. Because the alternative is working hard for no financial reward.

Recent findings suggest that how do you know if you can survive? Run through this quick checklist:.

Recent findings suggest that so how long will the pain last? History offers some comfort, provided you have the patience of a parent waiting for a toddler to put on his shoes while already 15 minutes late.

According to Capital Group, the S&P 500 has dropped 10% or more about once every 18 months since 1954. A 20%+ bear market highlights up about once every six years.

In other words, if you strategy on a 40-year retirement, expect roughly 25 corrections and six or seven bear markets. Declines are the price of admission, not a sign the world is ending. Get used to them.

Source: Capital Group, S&P 500 data from 1954 through 2025.

In a recent development, hartford Funds, using Ned Davis Research data going back to 1928, counts 27 bear markets. Stocks fell 35% on average and took 289 days, or about 9.6 months, to hit bottom.

Bear markets were far more common during the Depression era. Since 1945, there have been 15, or one about every 5.1 years.

It has been revealed that two caveats before you get too comfortable. First, these figures measure peak to trough. Getting back to your old high takes longer. Second, the 1973 and 1980 bear markets each dragged on for more than 600 days. Averages are nice until you're living through the outlier.

But here's the part that should make everyone feel better. Every S&P 500 correction since 1929 has been followed by a recovery, and the average return in the first year after the bottom was 52%. And the recoveries are happening quicker now, if we include the 2025 Liberation Day and 2026 Iran War events.

Hartford also found that about 42% of the S&P 500's strongest days over the past 20 years occurred during bear markets. Sell in a panic and you'll likely miss the rebound.

My takeaway: In a realistic worst-case scenario, initiative on gutting out roughly 12 to 18 months of pain from peak to trough, with a longer tail to fully recover. That's why the one to two years of cash is fine, especially with interest rates still high.

The existential dilemma of a bear market is this:.

It has been revealed that the correct answer is to work less hard and YOLO more. Let me explain using a concept I call Return On Effort (ROE).

During a bull market, working less hard actually increases your Return On Effort because your investments provide most of the returns. Unless you have a sales job or some other role tightly correlated to performance, an extra 15 hours a week rarely moves the needle. You're better off riding the organization's growth.

It has been revealed that during a bear market, working hard to run in place or lose money makes even less sense. There's nothing you can do to stem declining consumer confidence, upcoming socialist policies, higher taxes, and so forth. Your boss isn't handing out raises while revenue is falling. See Google's collapse after having such a huge lead in the AI race.

It has been revealed that if anything, your extra effort earns you the privilege of doing the work of three colleagues who just got laid off. Congratulations on your 0% raise.

So you work less hard to protect your declining Return On Effort. Not because you're lazy. Because you're rational.

It has been revealed that with this logic in mind, who works the least? The unemployed, the traditional retiree, and the early retiree.

Therefore, so long as your investments can withstand the beating, you're going to be just fine. Psychologically, as a retiree, you must push yourself to do less and have more fun.

Industry observers note that happiness is relative. During a bull market, plenty of early retirees feel a twinge of FOMO watching former colleagues get promoted and cash fat RSU checks. During a bear market, that FOMO flips. Nobody envies the guy grinding through a reorg while his stock comp gets cut in half.

Whether you’re retired or still grinding away, a downturn offers some real perks.

1) Things get cheaper. When demand falls, so do prices for travel, hotels, and eventually real estate. Retirees with flexible schedules can travel off-peak and score deals that working parents can only dream about. Workers looking to buy their first home may finally face less competition.

2) You get to shop the sale. Retirees with passive income and a cash buffer get to buy when others are forced to sell. Workers get an even steadier advantage. Every paycheck and 401(k) contribution now picks up more shares at lower prices. Steady income plus a long time horizon makes you the natural buyer in a bear market.

It has been revealed that 3) Your kids get to buy the dip. I’ve written about how to use stock market downturns to make your kids millionaires. As a father, this is my favorite benefit of a bear market. Because the equity train finally stops long enough for kids to catch up and hop on board. A child has 50+ years of compounding ahead. A 30% drop today is a rounding error by the time they’re in their 50s.

Recent findings suggest that 4) Tax moves get better. Tax-loss harvesting offsets future gains. Roth conversions at depressed valuations mean you pay less tax on the same number of shares, and all the recovery happens tax-free.

5) The AI hedge is doing its job. Public AI stocks have gotten crunched. But there’s a flip side. If AI companies are struggling to justify their valuations, AI probably isn’t wiping out white-collar work as fast as everyone feared. That’s comforting for our kids, and for every worker wondering if their job will exist in 10 years.

According to recent reports, 6) You get humbled and build resilience. Being heavily overweight tech felt brilliant for years. Bear markets remind us we’re not as smart as we thought. My advice after every huge win is to go scrub all your toilets. Every downturn you survive makes you a calmer, better investor for the next one. If you’re still working, just make sure your emergency fund is solid, because layoffs tend to show up at the worst time.

According to recent reports, you can’t control tech volatility, interest rates, or who wins elections. But you can control how you spend your time during a downturn.

The market will eventually recover. It always has. When it does, the people who grinded through the downturn will be exhausted. Those of us who leaned into family, friends, and fitness will be well rested. Both groups will survive, which is what matters most.

According to recent reports, if you’ve been thinking about retiring, a bear market may be the best time to pull the trigger. It means that in spite of the carnage, your finances are strong enough for you to break free. Waiting for the next bull market can feel safer, but it’s backwards.

It has been revealed that if your finances can support retirement while stocks are down 20% or more, your blueprint has already passed the stress test. You’re not retiring on inflated numbers that could vanish in the next correction. And since bear markets don’t last forever, a recovery may carry your retirement forward with a tailwind instead of a headwind.

Recent findings suggest that compare that to the person who retires at the peak of a bull market, only to watch their portfolio drop 30% in the first two years. That’s sequence of returns risk at its worst.

So go play in the park. Take your kids to the beach. A downturn is the best time to enjoy the freedom you worked so hard to build, and maybe the best time to claim it.

How much of your portfolio would need to fall before you'd seriously consider going back to work? Do you agree that working less hard in a bear market is the rational move, or is that just a cop-out for the lazy? And for those still working, has the market selloff made you rethink how hard you're grinding? Are you using the downturn to fund your kids' investment accounts?

A tiger killed two farmers in separate incidents about five kilometers apart within 24 hours in the eastern corner of India’s Maharashtra state.

The following evening, Premila Mahadole, 40, was attacked while harvesting rice. Her body was later found in the field. Officials suspect it was the same tiger, but this has not been confirmed.

The back-to-back killings have thrown residents across the district into a panic, according to the Times of India. At this time of year, many are out in their fields harvesting rice at the edges of forests.

The death toll from human-animal conflicts in just this part of Maharashtra state has now risen to 35 in 2026, according to officials.

U.S. Trio Make First Snowboard and Ski Descent of a Near-7,000'er in Langtang

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).
  • The team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style.
  • Industry observers note that on the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).

The team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style. They summited on October 20 and rode/skied down via the same line on the south face, while American photographer Blake Gordon and Canadian cinematographer Leo Hoorn filmed from a high camp.

Industry observers note that on the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026. Photo: Nick Russell.

“The south face of Dorje was always the goal, and I’d been planning/dreaming of it for over two years,” Nick Russell told ExplorersWeb while on his way to the airport.

Sources indicate that the expedition reached base camp on October 6, shortly after an intense storm blanketed Nepal’s mountains with heavy snow. For them, however, the snow was a blessing rather than a curse.

“The cyclone gave our zone some much-needed snow down low, and on the face, it allowed a clean descent (no down climbing, no rappels),” Russell stated.

Sickness slowed the beginning of the expedition. “Three out of five of us, myself included, caught COVID,” Russell said. Luckily, the climbers recovered just as the weather cleared and winds dropped, followed by a string of perfect days.

After the descent. Photo: Nick Russell/Instgram.

Recent findings suggest that “Adam, Billy, and I all carried our own gear, set the tracks, and climbed in alpine style on the face,” Nick Russell remarked. The team had hired three Sherpa climbers (Dawa Geljee Sherpa, Kami Sherpa, and Nuri Sherpa) who helped the camera crew get their gear to a high camp, plus a base camp crew, outfitted by Shangri-La Nepal Trek.

High camp at 6,000m on the south face of Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram.

In a recent development, the line of ascent/descent followed the snow from below 4,500m to Camp 1 (4,900m) by crossing an icefall. According to the team, this was the only real crux of the ascent, due to overhead serac hazard. At least, the exposed section was short — less than an hour.

It has been revealed that on the first day of the summit push, the team continued to their high camp at 6,000m, below the col and at the base of the snowy face. Russell recalls the details of the climb as follows:.

The south face is quite steep and sustained above the bergshrund, with sustained 45-50˚ and pockets of 55º, we estimate. The face had seen so much sun [over] the past two weeks that the rising conditions were the biggest unknown of the entire project.

Sources indicate that we didn’t know whether or not it would be too icy to ride/ski until we got on the face. The snow was mostly firm, pretty much on the brink of being edge-able. It was two tool and crampon climbing the entire way, with no proper rests to take the pack off.

In a recent development, it took about 7.5 hours to climb the face, and we topped out around 1:30 pm. It took roughly 1.5 hours to descend, with breaks for the cameras to reset.

According to recent reports, A climber leaves almost no tracks in the hard snow on Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram.

According to recent reports, the three summiters started down from the top at the same time, Russell on snowboard and his partners on skis. It was anything but easy.

“The snow was more firm than I would have liked, but just edgeable enough to hold an edge,” Russell recalls. “Between the altitude, exposure below, steepness, and how firm it was, it was by far the heaviest line I’ve ever ridden.” He added that if the snow had been a little harder, they would have had to rappel down.

The hard snow on the upper sections. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram.

“You always hope for stable, boot-top powder, but that’s rarely the case at high altitude,” Russell explained. “Instead, you make the most of the conditions presented and try to do it as safely as possible.”.

He added: “The entire line was a no-fall zone; one lost edge, and it’d be over. Regardless of conditions, it was a dream for all of us to ride off the top of a peak in Nepal.”.

After a partial descent, the team spent the night at high camp, hoping to ride some interesting slopes they had spotted earlier, but finally decided to bail the next morning. “We were satisfied,” Russell stated. They continued on skis/snowboard all the way down to the moraines below Camp 1 around 4,500m.

In a recent development, childhood friends Fabrikant and Haas often partner up on major ski expeditions, mainly in Alaska but also in the Himalaya. They climbed and skied both Gasherbrums 1 and 2 without oxygen after climbing them in the same style in 2024, together with Brendan O’Neill.

“They are the strongest partners I’ve ever been in the mountains with,” said Russell, who has also climbed and snowboarded twice in the Indian Himalaya and twice in Nepal.

“I tried Dhaulagiri in 2022 with Blake Gordon and Dan Corn, but the difficult conditions that year coupled with the loss of Hilaree Nelson [who fell to her death while trying to ski down Manaslu] didn’t allow us to make very much progress,” Russell said.

“I’ve always dreamed of riding lines in the Himalaya, and this felt like a major step forward in my personal journey,” he concluded.

While this is the first ski and snowboard descent of Dorje Lhakpa’s south face, the legendary Marco Siffredi snowboarded the west ridge of the mountain in 1999, with Bertrand Delapierre. Siffredi perished shortly afterward on the Hornbein Couloir on Mount Everest. “Dorje Lhakpa first entered my psyche from Marco and Bertrand’s descent,” the rider recalled.

The south face of Dorje Lhakpa was only climbed for the first time in 2021, by Spaniards Mikel Inoriza, Iker Madoz, and Mikel Zabalza.

According to recent reports, “I came across a photo of the south face and the American Alpine Journal article from the Spanish team’s first ascent in 2021,” Russell remarked. “The massive south face is visible from the Kathmandu Valley on a clear day, and it is honestly crazy to me that no one had skied it before.”.

In a recent development, “Today,” he went on, “people are so hyper-focused on the 8,000m peaks (for good reason, I get it), but there are still virgin lines waiting for a snowboard/ski descent in the 6,000-7,000m range. It just takes a shit ton of work to make it happen.”.
